unit.title: AI images, video and voice
unit.description: Midjourney, GPT Image, Flux, image prompts, reference and consistency, inpainting, upscaling, Sora and Veo, voice cloning, copyright, AI labels, seeds

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Each tool has a strength: Midjourney for aesthetics, GPT Image (OpenAI) and Nano Banana (Google) for following precise instructions and editing, Ideogram for legible text, Flux and Stable Diffusion as open weights for control and automation.
cards.example: A poster with a tagline: Ideogram 3 or GPT Image render the text without mistakes; Midjourney v7 will give the most beautiful image but often garbled letters.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A good image prompt describes, in order, the subject and its action, the style, the composition (framing, angle), the lighting, then technical parameters such as the aspect ratio. Concrete and visual rather than long.
cards.example: "Product photo of a handmade candle on an oak table, editorial style, tight shot, late afternoon natural light, blurred background --ar 4:5" for an Instagram post.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: An image given to the model steers the style (--sref in Midjourney) or locks a character, product or mascot that must reappear from one visual to the next (Omni Reference, GPT Image editing, a LoRA trained on the brand).
cards.example: An SMB trains a Flux LoRA on 30 photos of its flagship bag and passes its 2025 visual as --sref: every generated image shows the right logo, the exact camel color and the same midnight blue palette.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Inpainting regenerates a selected area of an image (removing an object, fixing a botched hand); outpainting extends the image beyond its edges to change format without cropping the subject.
cards.example: Your square visual must become a 16:9 banner: outpainting invents the missing sides (Photoshop Generative Expand, Flux Kontext), then inpainting erases a sixth finger.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Most generators output 1 to 2 megapixel images (up to 4K for the newest), too small for print. Upscaling (Magnific, Topaz, Midjourney's built-in upscaler) multiplies the resolution while reconstructing the details.
cards.example: A 1024 × 1024 px Midjourney image upscaled x4 gives 4096 px: enough for an 80 cm roll-up banner at 130 dpi, whereas the original pixelated from 20 cm wide.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Sora 2, Veo 3, Runway Gen-4 and Kling produce 5 to 15 second clips from a text or an image, Sora 2 and Veo 3 with synchronized sound. Limits: sometimes wrong physics, unreadable text, hard continuity between shots.
cards.example: For a 30 s ad, you generate 5 to 6 shots of 8 s from the same reference image, then edit: each shot costs from a few tens of cents to a few euros depending on the tool.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: ElevenLabs recreates a voice from one minute of audio (instant clone) or 30 minutes for a professional clone verified by voice captcha. Without the person's written consent, use violates their personality rights and the terms of service.
cards.example: A brand has its voice-over actress sign a cloning license (duration, media, fee), then rolls out the same voice in 30 languages for its ads.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: An image produced by a prompt alone is not protected by copyright, neither in the US (Thaler v. Perlmutter, 2025) nor in Europe: a creative human contribution is required. What you may do with it depends on the tool's terms.
cards.example: Midjourney grants usage rights to paying subscribers but requires the Pro plan for companies above 1 million dollars in revenue; a competitor can copy your raw visual without infringement.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The AI Act (Article 50, applicable since 2 August 2026) requires disclosing deepfakes and marking generated content in a machine-readable way. Meta, TikTok and YouTube add their own labels through C2PA Content Credentials.
cards.example: A fake AI-generated customer testimonial posted on Instagram without a label exposes the brand to the AI Act and to removal by Meta; a stylized illustration of a concept simply needs to carry the marking.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: You generate in batches of 4 variations, keep the best one and lock its seed so you change only one parameter at a time. Each image costs 2 to 20 cents via API: fast iteration is cheap, unmethodical iteration is expensive.
cards.example: 20 prompts × 4 variations × 3 rounds = 240 images, about 10 dollars with GPT Image at medium quality, versus 1,500 euros for a one-day photo shoot.

exercises.prompt: Your SMB wants a poster with the tagline "Summer sale -30%" perfectly legible. Which tool should you favor?
choices: Ideogram or GPT Image, strong at rendering text
Midjourney, the tool with the most aesthetic output
An upscaler such as Magnific or Topaz, for sharpness
Stable Diffusion 1.5 locally, without a LoRA
exercises.explain: Ideogram and GPT Image render text without mistakes; Midjourney is stronger on aesthetics but often garbles letters, and an upscaler generates nothing.

exercises.prompt: In the prompt "Product photo of a candle, editorial style, tight shot, soft light --ar 9:16", what does "--ar 9:16" control?
choices: The aspect ratio of the image, here vertical for a story
The number of variations generated on each run
The final resolution of the image, in pixels per inch
The intensity of the editorial style asked for in the prompt
exercises.explain: --ar sets the width:height ratio; 9:16 is the vertical format of stories and reels. Resolution and number of variations depend on other settings.

exercises.prompt: Your square visual must become a 16:9 banner without cropping the product. Which technique should you use?
choices: Outpainting, which extends the image beyond its edges
Inpainting, which regenerates a masked area inside the image
An x4 upscale to gain pixels on the sides
A --sref reference image of the square visual
exercises.explain: Outpainting invents the missing areas outside the frame; upscaling raises resolution without changing the ratio, and --sref only transfers style.

exercises.prompt: An agency generates a visual with a single prompt and no editing at all. Which statement is correct?
choices: Use allowed by the terms, but the raw image isn't protected
It holds full copyright over the image it generated
Copyright belongs to the publisher of the tool used
The image can never be used for commercial purposes
exercises.explain: Without a creative human contribution there is no protected work: ruled in the US (Thaler v. Perlmutter, 2025), same logic in EU law, which requires a person's own intellectual creation. Commercial use remains possible if the terms allow it, often tied to a paid plan.

exercises.prompt: With the same model, the same prompt and the same seed, you get a nearly identical image, which lets you change only one parameter at a time.
exercises.explain: The seed fixes the starting noise of the diffusion: with model and prompt unchanged, the result is reproducible, which is why it is used to test a single variable.

exercises.prompt: A company can clone a former employee's voice with ElevenLabs from his voice-over recordings, since they were made during his contract.
exercises.explain: The voice is a personality attribute: without written consent explicitly covering cloning, the use is unlawful and breaches ElevenLabs' terms, which require verification.

exercises.prompt: Put the workflow for producing a campaign visual with AI back in order.
steps: Brief and moodboard: subject, style, ratio, brand constraints
Generate in batches of 4 variations and select the best one
Lock the seed and the reference image to produce consistent variants
Fix with inpainting, extend with outpainting, then upscale
Add the AI label and Content Credentials, then publish
exercises.explain: You frame before generating, explore widely then lock (seed, reference), retouch and enlarge last, and transparency comes before publishing.

exercises.title: AI campaign visuals without legal risk
exercises.scenario: Boréal Cosmétiques, a 25-employee SMB, wants to produce 40 visuals and 3 clips of 8 s for its back-to-school campaign with AI, with no photo shoot budget. Management demands zero legal risk.

steps.prompt: Which tool and which plan should you choose to generate the visuals?
choices: A paid plan whose terms allow commercial use, terms archived
Midjourney's free plan: the visual result is identical
An open-weights model found on a forum, without reading its license
Stock photos edited with AI, without buying a license
steps.feedback: Midjourney's free plan imposes a CC BY-NC (non-commercial) license, and an open-weights model such as FLUX.1 [dev] is restricted to non-commercial use: it is the paid plan's terms that grant commercial usage rights.

steps.prompt: Marketing suggests featuring a well-known influencer and cloning an actor's voice for the voice-over. What do you answer?
choices: Refuse without a contract: fictional mascot and a licensed voice
Accept, because a generated face is never an exact copy
Accept on condition that you add the "AI-generated" label
Accept for the voice only, since voices are not protected
steps.feedback: Likeness and voice are personality rights: the AI label does not replace consent. A fictional mascot and a voice under written license remove the risk.

steps.prompt: The 40 visuals and 3 clips are ready. What should you do before publishing?
choices: Label the AI content and keep the Content Credentials
Strip the C2PA metadata so it goes unnoticed
File the raw images with the IP office to obtain copyright
Publish without a label, since these are not political deepfakes
steps.feedback: The AI Act and the platforms require transparency; stripping metadata exposes you to sanctions, and no filing protects an image without human contribution.

exercises.explain: Zero legal risk = commercial license through the right plan, written consent for any real face or voice, transparency about AI origin and clarity about the lack of copyright on raw images.

unit.title: Machine learning basics
unit.description: Supervised vs unsupervised, classification vs regression, features and labels, confusion matrix, clustering, random forests, reinforcement, bias-variance

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: In supervised learning, the model learns from examples that are already labeled (input + correct answer). In unsupervised learning, it gets raw data with no answers and must find structure on its own.
cards.example: Supervised: 50,000 emails tagged "spam" or "not spam" to train a filter. Unsupervised: 200,000 customer tickets automatically grouped by theme, with no predefined category.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Two families of supervised problems. Classification predicts a category (yes/no, cat/dog, A/B/C). Regression predicts a continuous numeric value (a price, a duration, a revenue figure).
cards.example: "Will this customer cancel?" is classification (yes/no). "How much will they spend over the next 12 months?" is regression (for example 347 €).

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Features are the input variables that describe each example (age, number of purchases, country). The label is the answer to predict. Choosing and preparing good features (feature engineering) often matters more than the choice of algorithm.
cards.example: To predict churn: features = tenure (months), number of support tickets, days since last login, monthly amount; label = "cancelled within 90 days" (1 or 0).

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The data is split into three parts: the training set fits the model, the validation set is used to choose its settings, and the test set measures final performance once, on data never seen before.
cards.example: Classic 70 / 15 / 15 split: out of 20,000 customers, 14,000 to train, 3,000 to validate, 3,000 to test. If the test set is reused to tune the model, its score no longer means anything.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A table that cross-tabulates predictions and reality: true/false positives, true/false negatives. Precision = share of predicted positives that are correct; recall = share of real positives found; F1 is their harmonic mean.
cards.example: A model flags 100 customers as "at risk": 60 really cancel (precision 60%). There were 200 real cancellations and it found 60 (recall 30%). F1 = 2 × 0.6 × 0.3 / (0.6 + 0.3) = 0.4.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Unsupervised method that groups data into clusters of similar items, with no labels. The k-means algorithm picks k centers, assigns each point to the nearest center and recomputes the centers until they stop moving.
cards.example: Segmenting 80,000 e-commerce customers by purchase frequency, average basket and recency with k = 4 reveals, for example, "premium loyal", "occasional", "deal hunters" and "dormant".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A decision tree chains simple questions ("tenure < 6 months?") down to a prediction: readable, but it overfits quickly. A random forest trains hundreds of trees on random subsamples and takes a vote: much more robust.
cards.example: In Python: scikit-learn's RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300). On tabular data (CRM, sales), forests and gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) still often beat neural networks.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Linear regression fits the straight line that best matches the data to predict a continuous value. Logistic regression pushes that line through an S-shaped function (sigmoid) to output a probability between 0 and 1: it is a classifier.
cards.example: Linear: sales = 1,200 + 3.5 × ad budget (in €). Logistic: P(churn) = 0.82 for a customer with 4 support tickets and 45 days without logging in; above the 0.5 threshold, they are classed "at risk".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: An agent learns by trial and error: it acts in an environment, receives a reward or a penalty, and adjusts its strategy (policy) to maximize cumulative reward. No labeled examples, only a feedback signal.
cards.example: AlphaGo learned by playing millions of games against itself. In marketing, a "multi-armed bandit" tests several email subject lines and gradually shifts traffic to the one getting the most clicks.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A model that is too simple has high bias: it underfits and misses even the training data. A model that is too complex has high variance: it overfits and collapses on new data. The right model sits in between.
cards.example: Accuracy of 62% on training and 61% on test: underfitting, the model is too simple. 99% on training and 70% on test: overfitting, it memorized instead of generalizing.

exercises.prompt: Predicting the amount in euros a customer will spend next year is a problem of…
choices: Regression
Classification
Clustering
Reinforcement learning
exercises.explain: The target is a continuous numeric value (an amount), not a category: that is regression. Classification would predict, for instance, "will spend more or less than 100 €".

exercises.prompt: Your model shows 98% accuracy on the training set but 65% on the test set. What is going on?
choices: Overfitting: high variance, it memorized the training data
Underfitting: high bias, the model is far too simple
The test set is too large compared with the training set
The model lacks the features it needs to learn
exercises.explain: A large gap between training and test is the signature of overfitting: the model fits the noise of the data it has seen and generalizes poorly. Underfitting would give a low score everywhere.

exercises.prompt: Out of 1,000 customers who really cancelled, your model spotted 400. Which metric is therefore 40%?
choices: Recall
Precision
The F1 score
Accuracy
exercises.explain: Recall measures the share of real positives the model finds: 400 / 1,000 = 40%. Precision would instead look at how many customers flagged "at risk" really cancelled.

exercises.prompt: What is the validation set for?
choices: Comparing model settings without touching the test set
Training the final model on a larger amount of data
Measuring the final performance quoted in the report
Labeling the data by hand before training
exercises.explain: The validation set is used to choose between several versions or settings of the model. The test set stays untouched until the end to give an honest measure on data never seen before.

exercises.prompt: The k-means algorithm needs labeled data to form its clusters.
exercises.explain: False: k-means is unsupervised. It groups points by proximity without any labels; it is then up to a human to interpret and name the resulting clusters.

exercises.prompt: A random forest takes a vote among many trees trained on different subsamples, which makes it less prone to overfitting than a single decision tree.
exercises.explain: True: each tree makes its own mistakes, but they cancel out in the vote. That is the principle of ensemble methods, very effective on tabular data.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a supervised machine learning project in order.
steps: Define the label to predict and gather the features
Split the data into training, validation and test
Train the model on the training set
Compare settings using the validation scores
Measure final performance once on the test set
exercises.explain: First decide what you predict and with what, split before any training to avoid leaks, tune on the validation set and only touch the test set at the very end.

exercises.title: Predicting subscriber churn
exercises.scenario: You are the CRM manager of a monthly subscription box: 40,000 subscribers, 4% cancellations per month. Management wants a model that spots at-risk subscribers one month ahead so they can be sent a retention offer. You have 3 years of history in the CRM.

steps.prompt: How do you frame the problem?
choices: Supervised classification, with "cancelled within 30 days" as label
K-means clustering to discover groups of similar subscribers
Linear regression on the amount spent per subscriber
Reinforcement learning, using clicks as the reward signal
steps.feedback: You have already-labeled history (who cancelled, when) and a binary target: the textbook case for supervised classification. Clustering does not predict anything, it describes.

steps.prompt: Your first logistic regression shows 96% accuracy on the test set. A colleague wants to deploy it right away. What do you think?
choices: Misleading: with 4% churn, "stays" for all already gives 96%
Excellent score, well above the 90% target: deploy it
You first need to switch to a deep neural network
You need to retrain on the test set to confirm
steps.feedback: On imbalanced classes, accuracy tells you nothing. The confusion matrix reveals whether the model really finds future cancellations (recall) without drowning the team in false positives (precision).

steps.prompt: Your final random forest reaches 45% precision and 70% recall. The retention budget allows contacting 800 subscribers per month. What do you do?
choices: Contact the 800 most at risk, with a control group to measure
Contact every subscriber predicted "at risk", whatever the number
Wait until the model reaches 100% precision before acting
Lower the threshold to 0.1 so no cancellation is missed
steps.feedback: The model outputs a probability: you use it to prioritize under a budget constraint. The control group is essential, otherwise there is no way to know whether the offer saved subscribers or whether they would have stayed anyway.

exercises.explain: A successful churn project relies on three reflexes: framing the problem well (supervised classification with a clear label), judging the model with the right metrics (precision, recall, F1 rather than accuracy on imbalanced classes), then linking the prediction to a measurable action.

unit.title: Everyday AI: tools and automations
unit.description: Choosing an assistant, memory and projects, meeting notes, Copilot and Gemini, Zapier, Make, n8n, deep research, vibe coding, confidentiality, fact-checking, team templates

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A chat app (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot) that answers, writes, summarizes and analyzes files. They are often close in quality: pick by your company's ecosystem, the task type and the data policy.
cards.example: Company on Microsoft 365: Copilot, already inside Outlook and Teams. On Google Workspace: Gemini. Long documents and careful writing: Claude. Images, voice and a consumer app ecosystem: ChatGPT. Pro plans run at roughly $20 to $30 per user per month.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Three settings so you stop re-explaining everything each chat: custom instructions (tone, job, format), memory (the assistant keeps facts across sessions) and projects, workspaces that group files, guidelines and chats about one subject.
cards.example: A Claude project called "Client Durand" holds the style guide (PDF), the last 3 meeting notes and the rule "answer in French, short email format". Every new chat in the project starts with that context. Equivalents: Projects in ChatGPT, Gems in Gemini.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: An assistant transcribes the video call live, then produces a summary, the decisions and the action items with an owner. Built into Teams, Meet and Zoom, or provided by dedicated tools such as Otter, Fireflies or tl;dv.
cards.example: A 45-minute Google Meet with "Take notes with Gemini" on: at the end, a Google Doc lands in the organizer's Drive with the summary and 6 action items. Golden rule: tell participants the meeting is being recorded and transcribed.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Microsoft 365 Copilot and Gemini for Google Workspace put AI straight into Word, Excel, Outlook, Docs, Sheets or Gmail. The benefit: the assistant reads your emails, files and calendar with your own access rights, no copy-paste needed.
cards.example: In Outlook: "Summarize this 27-email thread and list what is expected from me". In Sheets: "Add a column classifying these 400 customer comments as positive, neutral or negative". Microsoft 365 Copilot costs $30 per user per month; Gemini has been bundled into Workspace Business plans since 2025.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Zapier, Make and n8n chain apps without code: a trigger (new email, form, added row) launches actions, including an AI step that classifies, summarizes or writes. n8n is open source and self-hostable, useful for keeping data in-house.
cards.example: Make scenario: new Zendesk ticket → an OpenAI module assigns a priority and a category → a row is created in Google Sheets → a Slack message fires if priority is "urgent". Cost per run: a few cents, executed 200 times a day.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A mode where the assistant browses dozens of sites for several minutes, cross-checks sources and delivers a structured report with citations. Available in ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity, it replaces a morning of research, not your analysis.
cards.example: "Compare the 5 main accounting-firm management tools in France: pricing, integrations, 2026 reviews, with links." After 8 minutes, a 3-page report cites 34 sources. You open the 5 pricing links yourself before putting them in your proposal.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Cursor, GitHub Copilot and Claude Code write, fix and explain code from a natural-language request. "Vibe coding" (a term coined by Andrej Karpathy in 2025) means describing what you want and letting the AI code; great for a prototype, risky in production without review.
cards.example: A marketing manager with no dev background asks Claude Code: "Write a script that reads export.csv and sends a weekly email with the 10 most viewed pages". Working in 20 minutes. Before plugging it into real data, a developer checks error handling and access rights.

cards.subject: ia
cards.term: AI usage policy and confidential data
cards.definition: Internal rules stating which tools are allowed and what may be typed into them. Principle: never paste customer data, contracts, source code or personal data into a free or personal account; only into an enterprise plan where data is not used for training.
cards.example: In 2023, Samsung engineers pasted confidential source code into ChatGPT; the company banned the tool. Today a typical policy reads: "ChatGPT Enterprise and Microsoft 365 Copilot allowed; anonymize customer names; no HR files; no exports to personal accounts".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The habit of checking every figure, name, date, quote or legal reference produced by an AI before it reaches a client. The assistant can invent a credible-looking source; accountability for what is published stays with the human.
cards.example: In 2023, two New York lawyers were sanctioned for citing 6 court rulings that ChatGPT had made up. Simple method: ask for links, open them, and flag every unsourced figure in the draft as "to verify".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A reusable prompt with fill-in variables ({client}, {goal}, {tone}), tested and shared in a common space (Notion, shared project, team GPT or Gem). It standardizes quality and stops everyone from reinventing the instruction.
cards.example: "Customer review reply" template: "You are {brand}'s customer service. Reply to this {rating}/5 review in under 80 words, {tone} tone, no refund promises. Review: {text}". Versioned (v1.3), with 2 examples of a good reply and a named owner.

exercises.prompt: Your company runs entirely on Google Workspace and wants an assistant that reads emails and the calendar without copy-paste. Which choice makes the most sense?
choices: Gemini for Workspace, built into Gmail, Docs and Meet
Microsoft 365 Copilot, because it reads every file format
Free ChatGPT, pasting each email into the chat
Cursor, because it handles files on disk
exercises.explain: The assistant built into your suite accesses your data with your own rights, without moving it out. Copilot is the Microsoft counterpart; pasting emails into a free account is a data leak.

exercises.prompt: In every chat you repeat "you are our copywriter, direct tone, French, emails of 5 lines max". Which feature fixes this?
choices: Custom instructions, or a project with saved guidelines
Deep research mode, which keeps the context between chats
A Make scenario that pastes the text into an OpenAI module
A bigger model, which remembers instructions better
exercises.explain: Custom instructions apply to every chat; a project (ChatGPT, Claude) or a Gem (Gemini) scopes them to one subject, with the relevant files.

exercises.prompt: An SMB wants to automate "new form received → AI qualifies the lead → row in the CRM → Slack alert", but requires that data stay on its own servers. Which tool fits best?
choices: Self-hosted n8n on the company's own servers
Zapier, because it offers more than 8,000 apps
Otter, specialized in transcription
Perplexity in research mode
exercises.explain: Zapier and Make are cloud services: data passes through them. n8n can run on your own server, which meets the data-residency requirement.

exercises.prompt: A deep research report gives you a competitor's price with a link. What do you do before putting it in a sales proposal?
choices: Open the link and check that the page really shows that price, on that date
Insert it as is: the report cites 34 sources, so it is reliable
Ask a second assistant whether it agrees
Lower the temperature to avoid errors
exercises.explain: A citation can be misread, outdated or fabricated. A second model can repeat the same mistake; only the primary source, opened and dated, counts in a client document.

exercises.prompt: With a free personal ChatGPT account, you can paste a client contract to summarize it, since the conversation is private.
exercises.explain: On a free or personal account, data may be used for training and sits outside the company's control. Client documents go only through an enterprise plan covered by a contract.

exercises.prompt: Vibe coding lets a non-developer produce a working prototype, but the code must be reviewed before going to production.
exercises.explain: Cursor, Copilot or Claude Code produce working code fast, but with no guarantee on security, error handling or access rights. Prototype yes, production only after review by someone who understands the code.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for creating a prompt template shared with your team in the right order.
steps: Spot a task repeated by several people (review reply, brief, meeting notes)
Write the prompt with variables ({client}, {tone}) and 2 examples of a good result
Test it on 10 real cases and fix the instructions that fail
Publish it in the shared library with a version number and an owner
Collect feedback and update the version every quarter
exercises.explain: A template starts from a real need, gets tested before being shared, then lives on: the version number and owner keep the library from becoming a graveyard of stale prompts.

exercises.title: Nova Agency: meeting notes and tenders
exercises.scenario: Nova, a 25-person communication agency on Google Workspace, loses 15 hours a week writing client meeting notes and answers 4 tenders a month with hand-copied text. Management asks you for a plan to automate both without putting client data at risk.

steps.prompt: Decision 1: how do you produce the client video-call notes?
choices: Turn on Gemini note-taking in Meet, inform clients, then review and send the summary within 24 hours
Record with a free phone app on an intern's phone and paste the transcript into free ChatGPT
Send the generated summary to clients automatically, unreviewed, to save time
Ask Cursor to code an in-house transcription tool
steps.feedback: The tool built into the suite already in use keeps data inside the agency's account. Informing participants is mandatory, and human review remains the safeguard before anything goes to a client.

steps.prompt: Decision 2: how do you speed up writing tender responses?
choices: A shared project: 10 winning responses, the style guide, a template
Let each project manager write their own prompts in a personal account
Deep research on each tender, with the report sent as is
Generate the whole response in one prompt and sign it without review
steps.feedback: A project centralizes context (past responses, style guide) and a template keeps the tone consistent. The enterprise plan protects client documents; checking figures and references stays human.

steps.prompt: Decision 3: management wants incoming tenders received by email to be sorted and summarized automatically. How do you proceed?
choices: A Make or n8n scenario that extracts key info, tested on 20 emails
An assistant that reads each email and decides alone whether to reply
Forward the emails to a personal address for free ChatGPT
Hire someone full time to read all the emails
steps.feedback: A no-code automation with an AI extraction step is the right level: it sorts and summarizes, the human decides. Testing on past emails measures the error rate before going live.

exercises.explain: The winning plan combines three building blocks: AI built into the existing suite for meetings, a shared project with templates on an enterprise plan for tenders, and a tested no-code automation for email sorting. At every step, data stays under control and a human validates before anything reaches a client.

unit.title: Vision, voice and recommendation
unit.description: Computer vision, CNN, OCR, speech-to-text, TTS, recommendation, visual search, C2PA, deepfakes, edge AI

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The set of techniques that let a machine interpret an image. Three core tasks: classification (which object?), detection (where, with a bounding box) and segmentation (exactly which pixels).
cards.example: A YOLO model detects hard hats on a construction site in real time; Segment Anything (Meta) cuts a product out of its background in one click for a product page.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A neural network that slides small filters over the image to spot edges and textures first, then shapes, then whole objects. It learns those filters by itself during training.
cards.example: In 2012, AlexNet (8 layers) cut the ImageNet error rate from 26% to 16%. Today CNNs like ResNet coexist with Vision Transformers (ViT), which split the image into patches.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Optical Character Recognition: turning an image of text (scan, photo, PDF) into usable text. Modern OCR also reads tables, handwriting and page layout.
cards.example: Tesseract (open source) reads a clean receipt; Mistral OCR or Google Document AI extract the 40 lines of a scanned invoice as JSON, with amounts and VAT.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Speech recognition: converting audio into text. Recent models handle noise, accents and dozens of languages, and add timestamps, punctuation and speaker identification.
cards.example: Whisper (OpenAI, open source, trained on 680,000 hours of audio) transcribes a one-hour meeting in a few minutes; the text then feeds an LLM that writes the minutes.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Generating a voice from text. Neural models produce natural intonation, can clone a voice from a few seconds of audio and answer in real time within a conversation.
cards.example: ElevenLabs dubs a training video into 30 languages with the trainer's own voice; a voice support line chains speech-to-text, LLM and TTS with under one second of latency.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A recommendation method based on behavior: 'people who liked A also liked B'. By contrast, content-based filtering compares item attributes (category, color, description).
cards.example: Netflix attributes about 80% of viewing to its recommendations. A new item with no history ('cold start') is first recommended by its content, then by the clicks it collects.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Finding images from a photo or a text. A multimodal model like CLIP places images and text in the same vector space: a photo of a chair and the phrase 'wooden chair' end up close together.
cards.example: Google Lens handles close to 20 billion visual searches a month. On Zalando, you photograph a jacket seen in the street and the site shows the 20 closest items in the catalog.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: An open provenance standard: a cryptographic signature attached to the image says who created it, with which tool and which edits. It complements invisible watermarks, but vanishes if the metadata is stripped.
cards.example: Images generated by ChatGPT or Adobe Firefly, or shot with a Leica M11-P, carry Content Credentials; a screenshot removes them, which is why Google's SynthID watermark, embedded in the pixels, matters.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Spotting a synthetic face or voice: visual artifacts (blinking, reflections, lips), frequency analysis, trained detectors. No detector is 100% reliable: combine it with provenance and human verification.
cards.example: In 2024, an Arup employee in Hong Kong wired 25 million dollars after a video call where the 'CFO' and colleagues were all deepfakes. The fix: call back on a known number.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Running the model directly on the device (phone, camera, car) rather than in the cloud. Lower latency, better privacy, works offline, but with smaller, quantized models.
cards.example: Apple Intelligence runs a model of about 3 billion parameters on the iPhone using the Neural Engine; Gemini Nano summarizes a recording on a Pixel without sending the audio to Google.

exercises.prompt: You want to automatically cut each product out of its photos (isolate exactly its pixels). Which computer vision task is that?
choices: Segmentation
Classification
Detection
OCR
exercises.explain: Classification gives a label, detection a bounding box; only segmentation assigns each pixel to an object, which is what cutting out requires.

exercises.prompt: An item just entered the catalog: nobody has viewed or bought it yet. Which approach can recommend it from day one?
choices: Content-based filtering, from its attributes
Collaborative filtering, from similar purchases
A CNN trained on user clicks
None: you have to wait for 30 days of data
exercises.explain: This is the 'cold start' problem: with no history, collaborative filtering is blind. Content (category, color, description, image embedding) lets you recommend right away.

exercises.prompt: Why does a model like CLIP let you search photos with a phrase like 'black leather jacket'?
choices: It places images and text in the same vector space
It reads the text on clothing labels with OCR
It generates an image from the phrase and compares the pixels
It classifies each photo into one of ImageNet's 1,000 classes
exercises.explain: CLIP was trained on hundreds of millions of image-text pairs to bring an image close to its caption: that is what makes multimodal search possible without manual labels.

exercises.prompt: What is the main limitation of Content Credentials (C2PA) for proving that an image is AI-generated?
choices: They live in the metadata: a screenshot removes them
They add a visible logo that degrades image quality
They only work on videos, not on photos
They need a dedicated GPU to be read and checked
exercises.explain: The C2PA signature holds as long as the metadata stays; otherwise it vanishes. Hence the complementarity with a pixel-embedded watermark like SynthID.

exercises.prompt: In a convolutional network, the filters that detect edges and textures are hand-written by engineers.
exercises.explain: That is exactly the CNN breakthrough: the filters are learned automatically during training, from simple edges in the first layers to whole objects in the last ones.

exercises.prompt: Running a model as edge AI on the phone improves privacy and latency, but forces smaller models than in the cloud.
exercises.explain: Data never leaves the device and there is no network round trip, but memory and chip limit the size: a few billion quantized parameters, versus hundreds of billions in the cloud.

exercises.prompt: Put in order the steps of a voice assistant answering a customer on the phone.
steps: Capture the customer's audio
Transcribe the audio into text (speech-to-text)
Have the LLM generate the answer
Convert the answer into speech (TTS)
Play the audio to the customer and listen for what comes next
exercises.explain: The classic chain is audio, speech-to-text, LLM, TTS, audio. Each link adds latency: the goal is to stay under one second so the exchange feels natural.

exercises.title: Image Search and Recommendations for an E-commerce Site
exercises.scenario: You are advising an online fashion store (12,000 items, 30% new products every season). Management wants two features: 'photograph a garment and find it on our site' and personalized recommendations. Marketing would also like to produce visuals with AI.

steps.prompt: How do you build the image search?
choices: Index CLIP embeddings of the catalog, then compare the customer's photo
Run the customers' photos through OCR to read the brand on the label and search that keyword
Classify each photo into one of ImageNet's 1,000 classes and show all products in the same class
Compare the photos pixel by pixel against the catalog
steps.feedback: Embeddings capture shape, color and style regardless of framing and lighting. Bonus: the same index also answers text queries ('long floral dress').

steps.prompt: With 30% new products each season, which recommendation engine do you choose?
choices: A hybrid: content-based for new items, collaborative afterwards
Pure collaborative filtering: that is what Netflix and Amazon use
Show the top 20 bestsellers to everyone, it is simpler
Ask an LLM to pick in real time among the 12,000 items
steps.feedback: Collaborative filtering alone ignores new items (cold start) and bestsellers personalize nothing. The hybrid recommends from day one and sharpens with clicks.

steps.prompt: Marketing wants to generate AI visuals to save time. What do you recommend?
choices: Generate settings around the real product photo, approved by a human
Generate the products themselves from their description: no more photo shoots
Generate models imitating well-known influencers to boost conversions
Strip the metadata from generated images so nobody knows they come from AI
steps.feedback: A generated product never matches the item actually sold: seams, fabrics and logos drift, and returns skyrocket. Imitating a real person is a deepfake; hiding the origin breaches the AI Act's transparency obligations.

exercises.explain: One shared base of multimodal embeddings powers both visual search and content-based recommendation; collaborative filtering takes over as usage data arrives. For generation, AI dresses the product but never replaces it, and provenance stays visible.

unit.title: Branding and storytelling
unit.description: Brand platform, promise, guidelines, tone of voice, StoryBrand, aided / unaided awareness, ESOV, omnichannel consistency, Keller pyramid, rebranding

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Reference document that sets the mission (why the brand exists), the vision (the world it wants to create) and the values (how it behaves). Everything else, from logo to campaigns, must flow from it.
cards.example: Patagonia fits in one mission line: "We're in business to save our home planet". That line justifies the Worn Wear repair program and, since 2022, giving every profit not reinvested in the business to the fight against climate change.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Concrete commitment the customer can expect at every interaction. It turns the positioning (for whom, against what, with which benefit) into one verifiable sentence rather than a decorative slogan.
cards.example: FedEx built its brand on "When it absolutely, positively has to be there overnight": a measurable promise (delivered tomorrow), which every late parcel directly contradicts.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Rules for using the visual identity: logo and clear space, colors with exact codes, typefaces, imagery, layout. It ensures an intern or an agency produces the same brand as headquarters.
cards.example: Coca-Cola red is codified as Pantone 484 C / #F40009; Spotify publishes public rules on its site (green #1ED760, logo never distorted, minimum clear space equal to half the icon height).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: How the brand voice is modulated for each context: register, vocabulary, humor, level of formality. It is documented as sliders ("funny but not mocking") and varies from one message to the next, while the personality itself stays the same.
cards.example: Mailchimp's public guide (styleguide.mailchimp.com) separates voice (constant) from tone (variable): the same support team is playful in a welcome email and sober in a failed-billing alert.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Donald Miller's narrative structure (2017): the customer is the hero facing a problem, the brand is the guide who gives a plan and a call to action, with a success to win and a failure to avoid. The brand is never the hero.
cards.example: Payroll software homepage rewritten: "You spend 6 hours a month on payslips (problem). We automate them in 3 steps (plan). Start a free trial (call). Get your evenings back (success)."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Two survey measures. Unaided: "Which brands of X do you know?" (no list); the first named is top of mind. Aided: "Do you know brand Y?" (with a list). Unaided is always lower and harder to earn.
cards.example: A neobank surveyed by YouGov scores 62% aided awareness but 9% unaided: people recognize it when named, but do not think of it on their own. The TV campaign goal: lift unaided to 15%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Gap between share of voice (share of a category's media spend or mentions) and market share. Binet and Field's IPA work shows a positive ESOV predicts growth: roughly +0.5 market share point per year for every 10 points of ESOV.
cards.example: A coffee-pod brand holds 12% of the market but 20% of the category's ad spend: ESOV of +8. Its rival with 30% market share has only 22% SOV (ESOV of -8) and should lose ground over the medium term.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Same identity, promise and tone at every touchpoint: website, app, store, customer service, packaging, social. Each inconsistency costs recognition and trust; it is managed through a regular touchpoint audit.
cards.example: Apple: same SF Pro typeface, same white margins and same calm voice on apple.com, in the Apple Store app, on an iPhone box and in the in-store Genius script. You never find an "aggressive promo" tone on any channel.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Four-level brand equity model, bottom to top: salience (people know me), performance and imagery (what I do and what I stand for), judgments and feelings (what people think of me), resonance (loyalty and attachment). You cannot skip a level.
cards.example: An e-scooter brand invests in an ambassador community (resonance) while its unaided awareness sits at 4% (salience). By Keller's logic the money is misplaced: the base of the pyramid must be filled first.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Partial (refresh: logo, colors) or total (name, positioning) overhaul of a brand. Justified by a merger, a change of audience or offer, a damaged reputation; never by internal boredom. The rule: keep the distinctive assets the public recognizes.
cards.example: In November 2024 Jaguar unveiled a new logo and the line "Copy Nothing" without showing a car: the video drew millions of views but massive backlash, and European sales fell more than 90% in spring 2025 during the switch to electric.

exercises.prompt: In a brand platform, which statement describes the vision?
choices: The world the brand wants to help create in the long run
The brand's current reason for being, why it exists
The principles guiding day-to-day behavior
The logo's color and type codes
exercises.explain: The vision projects the desired future; the mission says why the brand exists today; the values say how it behaves. Color codes belong to the brand guidelines.

exercises.prompt: In the StoryBrand framework, which role should the brand play?
choices: The guide who gives the customer a plan to solve their problem
The hero whose success and values are told
The villain embodying the problem to fight
The neutral narrator describing product features
exercises.explain: In Donald Miller's model the customer is always the hero. The brand is the guide (like Yoda): it shows empathy, proves authority and provides a simple plan.

exercises.prompt: A survey asks: "Name the ride-hailing brands you know". 14% name your brand. Which measure is that?
choices: Unaided awareness
Aided awareness
Share of voice
Brand resonance
exercises.explain: With no list offered, respondents name brands from memory: that is unaided awareness. With a list ("do you know brand Y?") it would be aided awareness, always higher.

exercises.prompt: A brand holds 18% market share and 10% share of voice. According to Binet and Field, what should you conclude?
choices: ESOV of -8: it is under-investing and risks losing market share
ESOV of +8: it should gain about 0.4 share points per year
It is efficient: it spends less than its market weight
Nothing: share of voice only concerns social media
exercises.explain: ESOV = share of voice minus market share = 10 - 18 = -8. A sustained negative ESOV is associated with market share erosion, even if it looks "thrifty" in the short term.

exercises.prompt: A brand's tone of voice must stay strictly identical in a welcome message and in a security-incident notification.
exercises.explain: The voice (personality) is constant, but the tone adapts to context: you do not joke in a data-breach alert. That is the distinction Mailchimp documents in its guide.

exercises.prompt: According to Keller's pyramid, a little-known brand can offset its weak salience by investing directly in loyalty programs to create resonance.
exercises.explain: The pyramid is built bottom-up: without salience (being known and thought of at the right moment), there is nobody to make loyal. Resonance is the top, not a shortcut.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a well-run rebranding in order.
steps: Diagnose: measure awareness, perception and the distinctive assets the public recognizes
Rewrite the brand platform: mission, vision, values, positioning
Create the visual and verbal identity, then test it with customers
Train teams internally and prepare every touchpoint
Launch publicly while explaining the why, then track awareness and sales
exercises.explain: Measure before changing (so you do not discard a recognized asset), set substance before form, test before launch, and internal comes before external. Jaguar in 2024 reversed several of these steps.

exercises.title: Clarify the positioning before the raise
exercises.scenario: You are head of marketing at Fleeto, an 18-person startup selling fleet-management software to construction SMEs. In two months the founders pitch a Series A. Problem: the website says "the all-in-one mobility platform", the pitch deck says "AI telematics", and sales reps sell "fewer fines and less fuel". One investor already wrote: "I don't understand what you do or for whom". You have 8 weeks and 15,000 euros.

steps.prompt: Week one: what do you start with?
choices: Interview 10 customers and the sales reps to write a one-sentence promise
Commission a new logo and palette from an agency to modernize the image before the pitch
Launch a LinkedIn Ads campaign to raise awareness among investors
Keep all three messages: each channel speaks to a different audience, that is normal
steps.feedback: Substance before form. The problem is not the logo but the lack of a shared positioning. Customers will tell you in their own words what they really buy: that is the raw material of the promise.

steps.prompt: Interviews show customers mainly buy to "know where the trucks are and stop losing site hours". Which promise do you pick for the pitch and the website?
choices: "Fleeto gives construction SMEs back 5 site hours per truck per week"
"The next-generation AI mobility platform": more ambitious, investors like that
A different promise per persona (owner, site manager, accountant) so nobody is left out
The founders' story, two logistics-obsessed engineers, as the brand's heroes
steps.feedback: A promise fits in one verifiable sentence with a named audience and a quantified benefit. "Next-gen AI" jargon says nothing; several promises equal no promise; and in good storytelling the customer is the hero, not the founders.

steps.prompt: Four weeks and 12,000 euros remain. How do you roll out the new promise so the investor sees a consistent brand?
choices: Align homepage, pitch deck, sales script and LinkedIn on the same sentence
Put 12,000 euros into an emotional brand video on YouTube to build resonance
Change only the pitch deck: it is the only document the investor will read
Rename Fleeto, deemed too close to a competitor, at the same time as the message
steps.feedback: An investor checks the website, LinkedIn and calls customers: omnichannel consistency is the proof the positioning is real. A video targets resonance before the base (clarity) is laid; renaming 4 weeks before the pitch multiplies risk with no valid reason.

exercises.explain: Clarifying a positioning always follows the same path: listen to customers, write one unique verifiable promise, then repeat it identically at every touchpoint. Logo, video or name come later, and only if a real reason demands it.

unit.title: CRM and marketing automation
unit.description: HubSpot / Salesforce / Brevo, scoring, dynamic lists, workflows, lifecycle, CDP, GDPR, RFM

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Software that centralizes contacts, conversations, quotes and deals in one record per customer. HubSpot (free CRM, built-in marketing), Salesforce (enterprise leader, highly customizable) and Brevo (French, email-focused, SMB-friendly) are the most common.
cards.example: A 12-person SMB starts on free HubSpot: up to 1,000,000 contacts, sales pipeline and forms included, then upgrades to Starter (about 15 € per user per month) for automation.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A lead scoring grid that awards points based on declared profile (explicit: job title, industry, company size) and observed behavior (implicit: pages viewed, emails opened, demo requested). Above a threshold, the lead is handed to sales.
cards.example: Marketing director: +20. Company with 50+ employees: +15. Pricing page visit: +10. No email opened in 30 days: -5. MQL threshold set at 50 points.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A CRM segment that updates itself automatically from contact actions (clicks, purchases, pages viewed, inactivity) rather than fixed attributes. A contact joins or leaves the list as soon as their behavior changes, with no manual work.
cards.example: "Abandoned carts 7 days" list in Brevo: added a product to cart AND has not ordered in 7 days. It holds 340 contacts on Monday, 285 on Wednesday, with nobody editing it.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The three building blocks of an automation workflow. The trigger enrolls the contact (form submitted, purchase). The condition routes the path (if / else, delay). The action performs a task: send an email, update a property, notify a sales rep.
cards.example: Trigger: PDF guide downloaded. Condition: did the contact open email 1 within 3 days? Yes: send the case study. No: resend email 1 with a different subject line.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A series of automated emails, spaced a few days apart, that educate a lead who is not ready to buy yet: useful content first, social proof next, offer at the end. It stops as soon as the contact converts or crosses the scoring threshold.
cards.example: B2B sequence of 5 emails over 21 days: D0 guide, D3 article, D7 customer testimonial, D14 comparison, D21 demo invitation. Exit goal: 8% demo requests.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A 0 to 100 score computed by the CRM to estimate the risk that a customer leaves. It combines usage signals (fewer logins, unused features), support signals (open tickets) and billing signals (late payment) to trigger a retention action before cancellation.
cards.example: A SaaS sets an alert at 70: logins down 50% over 30 days (+30), 2 unresolved tickets (+20), no user added in 90 days (+25). At 75, the CRM creates a call task for customer success.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A CRM property that places each contact in the relationship: lead (left contact details), MQL (qualified by marketing), SQL (accepted by sales), customer (has bought), evangelist (recommends you). It drives which workflows and messages apply.
cards.example: In HubSpot, the "Lifecycle stage" property moves automatically from Lead to MQL when the score reaches 50, then to Customer when a deal closes. A customer with an NPS of 9 or 10 becomes Evangelist.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The CRM manages the relationship with identified contacts (records, conversations, sales). The CDP ingests data from every source (website, app, point of sale, ads, support), resolves identities and pushes unified profiles to activation tools, CRM included.
cards.example: A retailer connects Segment (CDP) to Salesforce: an anonymous visitor who becomes an in-store customer is matched with their 14 previous web visits, and their CRM record finally shows a full history.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Under GDPR, every marketing contact must rest on a legal basis documented in the CRM: free and explicit consent (no pre-ticked box), with date, source and the wording accepted. The CRM must also allow withdrawal, export and deletion of the data.
cards.example: Brevo properties on the record: "Marketing opt-in: yes, 12/03/2026, PDF Guide form, terms version 3.2". A click on "unsubscribe" flips the field to no and blocks every marketing workflow. Maximum fine: 4% of worldwide revenue.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A 1 to 5 score given to each customer on three axes: Recency (date of last purchase), Frequency (number of purchases in the period) and Monetary value (total spent). The resulting triplet, such as 5-5-5, builds segments like "champions" or "to reactivate".
cards.example: E-commerce over 12 months: Recency 5 if purchased within 30 days, 1 if more than 270 days. A 1-4-5 customer (big regular buyer, silent for 9 months) gets a -15% code; a 5-5-5 customer gets an invitation to the VIP program.

exercises.prompt: In an automation workflow, which building block enrolls a contact into the flow?
choices: The trigger, for example a form submission
The condition, for example "opened email 1"
The action, for example sending an email
The delay, for example waiting 3 days
exercises.explain: The trigger is the entry event. Conditions and delays then route the path, and actions perform the tasks.

exercises.prompt: A lead reached 50 points, then a sales rep called them and confirms a real need and a budget. Which lifecycle stage should be assigned?
choices: SQL: the lead is accepted and qualified by sales
MQL: they crossed the scoring threshold
Customer: the budget is confirmed
Evangelist: they gladly talk about you
exercises.explain: The scoring threshold makes them an MQL; qualification by a sales rep moves them to SQL. They only become a customer after buying.

exercises.prompt: Which capability sets a CDP apart from a classic CRM?
choices: Unifying data from every source into one profile, even anonymous at first
Storing contact records and the history of sales conversations
Sending automated email sequences based on behavior
Managing a sales pipeline with deal stages and forecasts
exercises.explain: Records, pipeline and emails are the core of a CRM. A CDP specializes in multi-source collection and identity resolution, then feeds the CRM and other tools.

exercises.prompt: On a 1 to 5 RFM grid, which customer deserves the VIP program invitation?
choices: Last purchase 4 days ago, 11 orders this year, 2,300 € spent
Last purchase 10 months ago, 9 orders this year, 2,100 € spent
Last purchase 3 days ago, 1 order, 45 € spent
Last purchase 5 days ago, 12 orders, 180 € spent
exercises.explain: Only the first customer is strong on all three axes (recency, frequency, monetary value), a 5-5-5 profile. The second needs reactivation, the third is new, the fourth buys often but little.

exercises.prompt: In a lead scoring grid, "visited the pricing page" is an explicit criterion.
exercises.explain: False. It is an implicit criterion, inferred from behavior. Explicit criteria are facts declared by the contact: job title, industry, company size.

exercises.prompt: Under GDPR, a pre-ticked "I agree to receive the newsletter" box on a form is valid consent.
exercises.explain: False. Consent must come from a clear affirmative act: the box must be unticked by default, and the CRM must keep the date, source and wording accepted.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for setting up automated nurturing in a CRM in the right order.
steps: Define the lifecycle stages and the point threshold that turns a lead into an MQL
Build the explicit and implicit scoring grid
Create the dynamic list of leads to nurture (valid opt-in, score below threshold)
Set up the workflow: trigger, conditions, actions and exit at the MQL threshold
Test on a sample, then measure the MQL conversion rate and adjust
exercises.explain: You first set the definitions (stages, threshold), then the measurement (scoring), then the audience (list), and only then the mechanics (workflow), which you test before rolling out.

exercises.title: An SMB automates its nurturing
exercises.scenario: Ludo Bureau, 15 employees, sells office furniture to businesses. One sales rep, 4,000 contacts in Brevo, including 800 imported from an old Excel file with no record of consent. Every month, 120 people download the guide "Designing an open space". The rep only has time to call 30 of them and picks at random.

steps.prompt: Which trigger and which exit should you choose for the nurturing workflow?
choices: Trigger: guide download with opt-in; exit: 50 points or quote request
Trigger: every contact in Brevo; exit: end of the 5 emails
Trigger: sales rep call; exit: none, the sequence loops forever
Trigger: any newsletter open; exit: only when they unsubscribe
steps.feedback: The guide download is the clearest interest signal, and exiting at the threshold or quote request avoids sending educational content to someone already ready to buy.

steps.prompt: After email 3, a lead reaches 55 points and has visited the "Quote" page twice. What should the workflow do?
choices: Take them out of the sequence, make them MQL and create a call task
Let them receive emails 4 and 5 so as not to rush them
Move them straight to Customer since they are looking at quotes
Reset their score to zero so they start again on a clean slate
steps.feedback: The threshold is crossed and buying intent is visible: time to hand over to a human. The rep now calls the 30 hottest leads instead of 30 random ones.

steps.prompt: What should be done with the 800 contacts imported from Excel with no record of consent?
choices: Exclude them and send one email to collect a dated opt-in
Add them to the workflow: they are professionals, GDPR does not apply in B2B
Bulk-set "opt-in: yes" to regularize the database
Keep them in the workflow but reduce the frequency to one email per month
steps.feedback: Without a documented legal basis, these contacts cannot receive automated marketing. A single, clearly identified re-permission email lets you rebuild traceable consent; the rest must be purged.

exercises.explain: Good automated nurturing combines a genuine-interest trigger, a handover to a human as soon as score and behavior justify it, and a contact base whose consent can be proven in the CRM.

unit.title: E-commerce and marketplaces
unit.description: AOV levers, cart recovery, Shopify vs WooCommerce, product page, Google Shopping feed, Buy Box, verified reviews, shipping, subscriptions, Product structured data

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Average order value is revenue divided by the number of orders. You raise it without extra traffic: bundles, a free-shipping threshold and complementary products suggested on the cart page.
cards.example: €42,000 in revenue over 1,000 orders = €42 AOV. A 'free shipping from €50' threshold nudges some customers to add a €10 item rather than pay for delivery.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An automated sequence (email, SMS, push) sent to identified visitors who left the checkout with items in their cart. It shows the product again, answers objections, and only offers a discount as a last resort.
cards.example: In Klaviyo: email 1 at H+1 ('Your cart is waiting'), email 2 at H+24 with customer reviews and a shipping FAQ, email 3 at D+3 with a 10% code. Such a flow typically recovers 3 to 8% of abandoned carts.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Shopify is a hosted SaaS platform: monthly subscription, maintenance included, paid apps. WooCommerce is a free WordPress plugin: total freedom, but hosting, security and updates are on you.
cards.example: A brand launching 200 SKUs picks Shopify (Basic plan around $29 per month billed yearly, Dawn theme, Shop Pay checkout). A WordPress blog selling 3 e-books simply adds WooCommerce.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The page that turns a visitor into a buyer. It combines multi-angle photos, a clear title, price and delivery time visible above the fold, benefits before specs, and answers to the main objections.
cards.example: A running shoe PDP: 6 photos and 1 video, size guide in a pop-in, 'Delivered Thursday if ordered before 2 pm', a returns FAQ. Adding the video lifted the add-to-cart rate from 8% to 11%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A file (CSV, XML or API) sent to Google Merchant Center that describes each product with standard attributes: id, title, description, link, image_link, price, availability, brand, gtin. It powers Shopping ads and free listings.
cards.example: Optimized title: 'Nike Pegasus 41 Men Running Black 43' rather than 'Pegasus 41'. Brand + model + gender + use + color + size: the searched words fit in the first 70 characters, the ones Google displays.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The 'Add to Cart' button on an Amazon listing shared by several sellers. Amazon awards it based on landed price, fulfilment method (FBA or Prime), order defect rate and stock availability.
cards.example: Over 80% of Amazon sales go through the Buy Box. A seller at €24.90 on FBA with a 0.4% order defect rate wins it against a seller at €23.90 who ships by himself in 6 days.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Reviews collected after a real purchase through a third-party platform (Trusted Shops, Trustpilot, Judge.me) or a marketplace. They reassure about the product and the store; well-handled negative reviews boost credibility.
cards.example: A page rated 4.3/5 on 210 reviews converts better than one rated 5/5 on 3 reviews. The merchant replies within 48 h to every review of 3 stars or less and shows customer photos under the description.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Shipping cost and delivery time often decide the purchase more than the product price. Fees discovered late at checkout are the top cause of abandonment; showing them on the product page and offering free returns limits the damage.
cards.example: According to Baymard Institute, 48% of abandonments come from extra costs seen as too high (shipping, taxes). A store moves from '€6.90 shipping' to 'free from €60': abandonment down 6 points, AOV up €9.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: For regularly consumed products (coffee, pet food, contact lenses), a subscription turns a one-off purchase into recurring revenue. Repeat purchases can also be triggered by a reminder sent just before the product runs out.
cards.example: Amazon Subscribe & Save gives 5 to 15% off in exchange for a scheduled delivery. On Shopify, the Recharge app runs a coffee subscription 'every 4 weeks, -10%'; a subscriber is worth about 3 times a one-off buyer over 12 months.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: schema.org markup in JSON-LD added to the product page: Product with name, image, Offer (price, priceCurrency, availability) and AggregateRating. Google uses it for rich results, and Merchant Center can read your products from it without a feed.
cards.example: {"@type":"Product","name":"Cafetière X1","offers":{"@type":"Offer","price":"89.00","priceCurrency":"EUR","availability":"https://schema.org/InStock"}}: price, stock and stars show up directly in the SERP.

exercises.prompt: A store makes €84,000 in revenue from 2,400 orders in a month. What is its average order value?
exercises.explain: AOV = revenue / number of orders = 84,000 / 2,400 = €35. To raise it: bundles, a free-shipping threshold, complementary products in the cart.

exercises.prompt: According to Baymard Institute studies, what is the number one cause of cart abandonment?
choices: Extra costs (shipping, taxes) discovered at checkout
The lack of a loyalty program or points to collect
Product photos that are poor quality or too few
An unprofessional logo that inspires little trust
exercises.explain: It is the number one reason, far ahead of the others: 40 to 50% of abandonments depending on the study's edition. Showing shipping cost and delivery time on the product page, or setting a free-shipping threshold, directly reduces this reason.

exercises.prompt: Four sellers offer the same product on Amazon. Which one is most likely to win the Buy Box?
choices: FBA seller, competitive landed price, 0.3% defect rate, in stock
Seller with the lowest price, but who ships by themselves within 8 days
Seller whose listing shows the most reviews
Seller who wrote the longest description
exercises.explain: The Buy Box is decided by landed price, fulfilment method (FBA/Prime), seller performance and stock. Reviews and the description belong to the shared listing, not to the seller.

exercises.prompt: Which attribute is required in a Google Merchant Center product feed?
choices: availability
sale_price
custom_label_0
product_highlight
exercises.explain: Required attributes are id, title, description, link, image_link, price and availability (plus brand and gtin when they exist). sale_price, custom_label and product_highlight are optional.

exercises.prompt: To convert, a product page should list every technical spec before the benefits, and place the delivery time at the bottom of the page.
exercises.explain: It is the opposite: benefits first, specs after, and price, stock and delivery time visible above the fold. Objections (size, returns) are handled next to the buy button.

exercises.prompt: A schema.org Product markup in JSON-LD, with Offer (price, currency, availability), can be read by Google Merchant Center to list your products without a separate feed.
exercises.explain: Merchant Center can crawl your site and build listings from Product structured data. The markup also powers rich results (price, stars) and must stay consistent with the page and the feed.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps to get your products on Google Shopping in the right order.
steps: Create the Google Merchant Center account and claim the website
Prepare the feed with the required attributes or mark up product pages with schema.org Product
Submit the products and fix the disapprovals flagged in diagnostics
Link Merchant Center to the Google Ads account to make the approved products available there
Launch the Shopping campaign and adjust bids based on margins
exercises.explain: Without a verified account nothing goes through; without approved products the campaign does not serve. Fix disapprovals (price mismatch with the page, missing image) before spending a single euro on bids.

exercises.title: The leaking checkout
exercises.scenario: You run a Shopify cosmetics store (AOV €38, 1,200 carts created per week). Three weeks ago the team redesigned the checkout and switched carrier. Since then, cart abandonment has jumped from 68% to 84%, while traffic and add-to-cart rate have not moved.

steps.prompt: What do you do first?
choices: Analyze the checkout funnel step by step to locate the drop
Immediately send a -20% code to the whole email list
Double the Google Shopping budget to make up for lost sales
Switch Shopify theme to modernize the whole store
steps.feedback: The checkout report shows 90% of the drop concentrated at the 'Shipping' step: the new carrier displays €7.90 shipping and 5 working days, and nothing announces it earlier. A discount or more budget would only have poured water into a leaking funnel.

steps.prompt: Which fix do you implement first?
choices: Show costs and lead times on the product page, free shipping from €45
Hide shipping costs until the payment page so visitors are not scared off
Make account creation mandatory so every abandonment can be followed up
Remove the order summary from the checkout to make it shorter
steps.feedback: No more surprise at the shipping step, and the €45 threshold (just above the €38 AOV) nudges people to add a product. Within two weeks abandonment falls back to 70% and AOV rises to €44. A mandatory account would have added friction: it is one of the top reasons for abandonment according to Baymard.

steps.prompt: 70% of carts are still abandoned. What recovery flow do you set up?
choices: Three messages: H+1 reminder, H+24 reviews, -10% at D+3 if no order
A single immediate email with -25% for every abandoned cart
Wait 7 days before any message so as not to seem pushy
Phone every single person who abandoned a cart, one by one
steps.feedback: The first message goes out while intent is still hot, the second reassures, and the discount only comes last so customers do not learn to wait for a code. The flow recovers 6% of carts, about 50 extra orders per week.

exercises.explain: When abandonment explodes: first locate the leak in the funnel, then remove the cause (hidden fees and delivery time), finally recover the remaining carts with a progressive sequence. A discount is a last resort, never a reflex.

unit.title: Local SEO and ASO
unit.description: Google Business Profile, local pack, NAP, reviews, local pages, ASO, store listing conversion, App Store vs Play Store, listing A/B tests

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Free listing that shows your business on Google Maps and in local results: name, category, address, hours, photos, reviews. It replaced Google My Business in 2021 and is managed straight from Google Search or Maps.
cards.example: A florist picks "Florist" as primary category, adds 20 photos, sets holiday hours and publishes one post a week: the listing shows up for "florist" in the neighbourhood.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Block of 3 listings with a map, shown at the top of results for a local query. Google ranks it on three official factors: relevance (category, listing content), distance from the searcher and prominence (reputation, reviews, links).
cards.example: For "plumber" searched from Nantes, the local pack shows 3 nearby, well-rated plumbers; the 4th only gets clicks on "More places". A plumber 15 km away, however good, does not make it in.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: NAP = Name, Address, Phone. A citation is any mention of those three details on a third-party site (Yelp, Apple Maps, Yellow Pages, directories). Strictly identical NAP everywhere reassures Google that the business exists at that location.
cards.example: "12 Pasteur Street" on the Google listing, but "12, Pasteur St." and an old phone number on Yellow Pages: an inconsistency to fix. Tools like BrightLocal or Semrush Listing Management flag these gaps.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Customer reviews (1 to 5 stars plus text) left on the Google Business Profile: they drive prominence in the local pack and the listing's click-through rate. Reply to every review; you cannot delete one, only flag it if it breaks Google's policies.
cards.example: A restaurant goes from 4.1 to 4.5 by asking for a review via a QR code on the bill and replies within 48 h to negative reviews with a concrete fix, never buying reviews (a practice Google penalizes).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.term: Local landing pages and geo-modified keywords
cards.definition: One dedicated page per city or branch, targeting "service + city" queries ("plumber Lyon 3"), with address, hours, map, reviews and unique content. It fuels local organic rankings and links to the matching Google listing.
cards.example: A chain of 40 gyms builds 40 pages such as /gym/toulouse, each with its own coaches, hours and LocalBusiness schema markup, instead of a single generic "Our clubs" page.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Optimizing an app's store listing so it gets found and then downloaded on the App Store and Google Play. Main levers: title, subtitle or short description, keywords, icon, screenshots, video, ratings and reviews.
cards.example: A meditation app renames its listing "Calmo: Meditation & Sleep" (title capped at 30 characters on both stores), redoes its first 3 screenshots and gains 30% more organic installs in two months.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Share of listing visitors who install the app. App Store Connect separates impressions, product page views and downloads; the Play Console reports store listing visitors and acquisitions. The icon and the first 2 or 3 screenshots matter most.
cards.example: 10,000 product page views and 2,800 installs = 28% conversion. Reaching 3,300 installs with no extra traffic (33%) cuts the cost per install by 15% across every campaign.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Average rating out of 5 and reviews shown on an app's store listing: a ranking and conversion signal. On Google Play the rating is computed per country and favors recent reviews; on the App Store it can be reset with each version. Both stores allow replies.
cards.example: Ask for an in-app rating right after a win (level completed, order delivered) via Apple's requestReview API (max 3 prompts a year) or Google's In-App Review API, never on first launch.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.term: Play Store vs App Store listing
cards.definition: On the App Store, search indexes the title (30 characters), the subtitle (30) and a hidden 100-character keyword field, not the description. On Google Play, the title (30), short description (80) and long description (4,000) are all indexed.
cards.example: Writing "free, fast, simple" in the long description helps on Play but does nothing on the App Store; there, every word of the keyword field counts, comma-separated without spaces, never repeating words from the title.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.term: Store listing A/B tests (Play store listing experiments)
cards.definition: The Play Console lets you test up to 5 variants of icon, screenshots, video or description on a share of traffic, measuring the impact on installs. Apple's equivalent, Product Page Optimization, compares up to 3 treatments against the original product page.
cards.example: Test on 50% of traffic for 2 weeks: the variant with screenshots captioned "Book in 10 seconds" delivers +8% retained installs with a fully positive confidence interval; it is rolled out to 100%.

exercises.prompt: What are Google's three official ranking factors for the local pack?
choices: Relevance, distance and prominence
Number of photos, domain age and Google Ads budget
Backlinks, site speed and HTTPS
Number of posts, message replies and online menu
exercises.explain: Google documents three factors: how relevant the listing is to the query, its distance from the searcher and its prominence (reputation, reviews, links). Ads budget has no effect on organic local ranking.

exercises.prompt: On Apple's App Store, which listing element is NOT indexed by search?
choices: The description
The subtitle
The 100-character keyword field
The title
exercises.explain: Apple indexes the title, subtitle and hidden keyword field, but not the description: it only serves to persuade. Google Play, by contrast, also indexes the short and long descriptions.

exercises.prompt: What does the acronym NAP stand for in local SEO?
choices: Name, Address, Phone: the business's contact details
Network, Authority, Popularity: the site's reputation
Note, Appraisal, Pictures: the Google listing content
Nearby, Active, Popular: the local pack criteria
exercises.explain: NAP covers the name, address and phone number. It must be written exactly the same way on the website, the Google listing and every directory (citation).

exercises.prompt: An App Store listing gets 20,000 product page views and 5,000 downloads. What is its product page conversion rate?
exercises.explain: 5,000 / 20,000 = 0.25, so 25%. This product page views to downloads ratio is the one you improve with the icon, screenshots and reviews.

exercises.prompt: On Google Play, the average rating shown for an app is the same in every country.
exercises.explain: Google Play computes and displays the rating per country (or region) and weights recent reviews more heavily. An app can be at 4.6 in France and 4.1 in Brazil.
