exercises.prompt: With Product Page Optimization, Apple lets you test up to 3 treatments of the product page on top of the original.
exercises.explain: Product Page Optimization compares the original against up to 3 treatments (icon, screenshots, app previews). On Google Play, a store listing experiment likewise tests up to 3 variants against the current listing, with up to 5 localized experiments running at once.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a Google Play store listing experiment in order.
steps: Pick a single element to test (icon, screenshots…) and write a hypothesis
Create the variant in the Play Console and set the share of traffic exposed
Let it run for at least 7 days until the result is statistically reliable
Apply the winning variant to 100% of traffic
Track the conversion rate over the following weeks to confirm the gain
exercises.explain: You test one element at a time to know what made the difference, wait for a reliable result before deciding, then check the gain holds outside the test.

exercises.title: The bakery nobody finds on Google Maps
exercises.scenario: Nadia opened the bakery "Au Levain" in Rennes 8 months ago. For "bakery Rennes" she appears nowhere, and even on her own name her listing shows up behind competitors in Maps. That listing, auto-created by Google, is unclaimed, shows wrong hours and has 3 unanswered reviews. Her website and Yellow Pages show a differently written address and an old phone number.

steps.prompt: What should she do first?
choices: Claim the listing, get it verified, choose "Bakery" and complete it
Launch a 500-euro-a-month local Google Ads campaign to compensate
Create a brand-new second listing to start from scratch
Rename the listing "Au Levain, best artisan bakery in Rennes"
steps.feedback: An unclaimed, incomplete listing cannot look relevant to Google. A duplicate creates a conflict, Ads do not fix organic ranking, and stuffing keywords into the name breaks the rules and risks a suspension.

steps.prompt: The website, Yellow Pages and Facebook show differently written addresses and an old phone number. What now?
choices: Align the NAP identically everywhere (website, Google listing, directories, social) and fix every wrong citation
Ask every third-party directory to remove the listing so only the Google one remains
Do nothing: Google will figure out it is the same business
Change the address on the Google listing to copy the Yellow Pages version, even if wrong
steps.feedback: Consistent citations build Google's trust and the listing's prominence. Removing them loses that signal, and an old phone number means missed customer calls.

steps.prompt: The listing has only 3 reviews, including an unanswered 2-star one. What strategy?
choices: Reply to all 3 reviews, then a QR code at the counter, no incentive
Buy 50 five-star reviews from a platform to catch up with competitors
Give a free croissant to every customer who leaves a 5-star review
Ignore reviews: only hours and address matter for Maps
steps.feedback: Reviews feed prominence and click-through rate. Buying reviews or rewarding a specific rating violates Google's policies (and consumer protection law); asking for an honest review is allowed.

exercises.explain: To escape local invisibility: a claimed, complete, well-categorized listing (relevance), a consistent NAP everywhere (trust), then steady reviews and replies (prominence). Ads and forbidden shortcuts replace none of these three building blocks.

unit.title: Video, influence and community
unit.description: 3-second hook, completion rate, YouTube SEO, live shopping, nano-influencers, brief and legal disclosure, UGC creators, moderation, EMV

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: On short vertical formats (TikTok, Reels, Shorts), the algorithm judges a video by its immediate retention. The hook is the visual or spoken opener packed into the first 3 seconds to stop the swipe.
cards.example: A skincare brand opens with "I went 30 days without moisturizer" and shows the result on screen; the logo waits until the end. Retention at 3 s: 78% versus 45% for the version that opened with the logo.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Share of views that reach the end of the video. Together with watch time (total minutes watched), it is the signal TikTok, YouTube and Instagram use to decide whether to push a piece of content to a wider audience.
cards.example: Out of 1,000 views of a 15 s Short, 900 reach the end: 90% completion. An 8-minute tutorial watched 2 minutes on average is rarely finished, yet generates 8 times more watch time per view. Both matter, depending on the format.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Optimizing a video for YouTube search and suggestions: keyword in the title (under 60 characters), a readable thumbnail that maximizes CTR, a description with timestamped chapters, then retention that confirms relevance.
cards.example: Title: "Assemble an electric bike in 20 minutes". Description with "0:00 Unboxing", "2:10 Front wheel", "9:45 Brake tuning": YouTube builds the chapters automatically. Thumbnail CTR rose from 3.1% to 6.4% after replacing the text with a face and a number.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Selling during a live video, with pinned products that can be bought without leaving the app (TikTok Shop, YouTube Shopping, Whatnot). It is the most direct form of social commerce: the creator demonstrates, the audience comments and buys.
cards.example: A 1-hour TikTok Shop live hosted by a beauty creator: 12,000 unique viewers, 640 orders, 34 € average basket (21,760 € in sales), with a "LIVE15" code valid only during the stream.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A creator with 1,000 to 10,000 followers (micro runs from 10,000 to 100,000). The audience is small but close: the engagement rate (interactions / followers) is often 3 to 5 times higher than that of a multi-million account.
cards.example: A supplements brand seeds 40 nano-creators (6% average engagement) instead of 1 macro with 800,000 followers (1.2%). For the same 8,000 € budget, the nanos generate 3 times more comments and 2 times more clicks to the site.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Document that frames a collaboration: goal, key messages, don'ts, deliverables (number of videos, formats, dates), content usage rights, exclusivity and fees. It is attached to the written contract, which French law requires above a certain amount.
cards.example: Brief from a coffee brand: "2 Reels + 3 stories between October 3 and 17, show the brewing, no health claims, 6-month usage rights for ads (whitelisting), 60-day coffee exclusivity, 1,200 € + 10% on the promo code".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Obligation to flag any sponsored content or gifted product. In France, the law of June 9, 2023 requires "Publicité" or "Collaboration commerciale" readable throughout the video; the US FTC requires a clear disclosure such as #ad. The platform label adds to it, not replaces it.
cards.example: A "#collab" buried among 20 hashtags at the end of the caption is not enough. Compliant version: on-screen text "Collaboration commerciale avec Marque X" from the first second of the Reel, plus the Paid partnership label. The French DGCCRF has already sanctioned creators for missing disclosures.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A creator paid to produce authentic-looking videos (unboxing, testimonial, demo) that the brand runs on its own accounts and in ads, without posting them on their own feed. It is a creator-economy job: you buy content, not audience.
cards.example: A DTC mattress brand orders 10 UGC videos at 250 € each (2,500 €) for its TikTok Ads. The best one gets a cost per purchase 40% lower than the 15,000 € studio ad, because it looks like native feed content.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Written rules that tell the community manager what to do with each comment: reply (question, reasoned criticism), hide (insult, spam, personal data), report or escalate (threat, crisis). It also sets the target response time and the brand tone.
cards.example: Guidelines of a clothing brand: reply within 2 hours during the day, never delete a quality complaint (answer publicly, then move to DM), hide external links, escalate to legal any comment mentioning an injury.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Theoretical value of the visibility earned through creators: each impression, view or interaction is multiplied by an equivalent media rate (for instance a CPM or a paid cost per view). Useful to compare campaigns, misleading if presented as revenue.
cards.example: 20,000 € campaign: 4 million views and a reach of 1.5 million unique people. At 0.02 € per view, EMV is 80,000 €; the actual cost per view is 0.005 € (20,000 / 4,000,000). The real business metric remains the 1,100 sales tracked through promo codes.

exercises.prompt: A 20 s TikTok video loses 60% of its viewers before the 3rd second. What is the priority fix?
choices: Replace the intro (logo, "hi everyone") with an instant hook
Extend the video to 60 s to increase total watch time
Add 15 hashtags to the caption to widen distribution
Post at 8 am instead of 6 pm to reach a more attentive audience
exercises.explain: A drop before 3 s is a hook problem, not a length or timing problem: the algorithm reads that early swipe as a negative signal and cuts distribution. Making the video longer would only hurt completion.

exercises.prompt: Two videos: A, a 15 s Short with 85% completion; B, a 10-minute tutorial with an average view duration of 4 minutes. What can you conclude?
choices: Each format has its own metric: watch time for B, completion for A
A will necessarily rank better than B, since its completion is higher
B is a failure, since 60% of the video is not watched on average
B should be cut into 40 Shorts of 15 s to reach 85% completion everywhere
exercises.explain: Completion rate mostly matters on short formats, absolute watch time on long ones. A 4-minute average view on a 10-minute tutorial is a very good result for YouTube.

exercises.prompt: For YouTube to automatically display chapters on a video, the description must contain:
choices: At least 3 timestamps, the first at 0:00, chapters of 10 s or more
The main keyword repeated 5 times in the first two lines
A link to the playlist and to the high-definition thumbnail
At least 10 hashtags, including one with the channel name
exercises.explain: Those are YouTube's three conditions for chapters. They then show on the progress bar and sometimes in Google as "key moments", which helps the video rank.

exercises.prompt: A creator receives a bag gifted by a brand, with no payment, and shows it in a Reel. What does French law say?
choices: A gift counts as compensation: "Collaboration commerciale" must show throughout
No disclosure is required, since no money changed hands
A #collab at the end of the caption is enough, as long as the Paid partnership label is also on
Disclosure is only mandatory above 10,000 followers
exercises.explain: The June 9, 2023 law covers any compensation, in cash or in kind, whatever the follower count. The mention must be clear, readable and present throughout the promotion; the platform label does not replace it.

exercises.prompt: A nano-influencer (1,000 to 10,000 followers) generally shows a higher engagement rate than an account with several million followers.
exercises.explain: True: the smaller and closer the audience, the larger the share of followers who interact. That is why brands activate dozens of nanos and micros rather than a single star.

exercises.prompt: The EMV of an influencer campaign equals the revenue generated by the creators.
exercises.explain: False: EMV values the visibility earned at an equivalent media rate. It is meant to compare campaigns; sales are measured with promo codes, tracked links or a post-purchase survey.

exercises.prompt: Put in order the steps to build the video editorial calendar of a launch with creators.
steps: Set the launch date and the goal (sales or awareness), then work the timeline backwards
Select the creators, send the briefs and sign the contracts (usage rights, legal disclosure)
Approve the videos and schedule the posts: teasers at D-7, launch at D0, UGC and live at D+7
Prepare community management: moderation guidelines, canned replies, on-call duty on launch day
Measure at D+30 (reach, completion, cost per view, sales by code) and adjust the next calendar
exercises.explain: The calendar starts from the target date and works backwards: no signed contracts, no videos to schedule; no moderation guidelines before D0, and the community is handled in a rush. Measurement closes the loop.

exercises.title: Launching a serum with creators
exercises.scenario: Noor, a DTC skincare brand sold only on its own site, launches a 39 € serum in 6 weeks. Influence budget: 15,000 €, targets TikTok and Instagram, goal: 800 orders in the first month. You run the campaign.

steps.prompt: Decision 1: how do you allocate the budget across creators?
choices: 20 engaged nano and micro skincare creators (4-6%) for 12,000 €, plus 5 UGC videos at 600 €
A single lifestyle macro-influencer with 1.5 million followers (1% engagement) taking the whole 15,000 €
50 creators picked only on follower count, without checking niche or engagement
No creators: shoot a studio ad and run it as YouTube pre-roll
steps.feedback: Good call: many niche creators with high engagement spread the risk and produce feed-native content; the UGC videos will feed the ads in the same style. A single lifestyle macro puts everything on one card with a poorly qualified audience.

steps.prompt: Decision 2: what goes into the brief and contract sent to the creators?
choices: A written brief (messages, don'ts, deliverables, rights) and a contract enforcing disclosure
A word-for-word script to read to camera, so the message is identical everywhere
No contract: creators are free, we just ask them to tag the brand
Ask them to avoid any partnership mention so the videos look more authentic
steps.feedback: Correct: the brief frames the substance without dictating the form, the contract secures usage rights to reuse the videos in ads and makes the legal mention non-negotiable. A read script kills authenticity; hiding the partnership exposes both brand and creator to sanctions.

steps.prompt: Decision 3: at D+30, the campaign totals 3.2 million views, a reach of 1.1 million, 60% completion on Reels, 900 orders through promo codes and critical comments about the price. What do you do?
choices: Compute cost per order (16.7 €), compare creators, answer price criticism, renew the 5 best
Present management with a 64,000 € EMV (3.2 million views × 0.02 €) as the campaign's revenue
Judge the campaign on view count alone and renew all 20 creators as is
Hide every critical comment about the price to protect the product image
steps.feedback: Well done: the 800-order goal is beaten and the 16.7 € cost per order on a 39 € serum stays profitable. EMV is for comparison, not for claiming revenue. Reasoned criticism is handled publicly per the moderation guidelines: hiding it would fuel distrust.

exercises.explain: A successful creator campaign combines high-engagement niche profiles, a clear brief with usage rights and flawless legal disclosure, then measurement based on cost per view, cost per order and real engagement, never on EMV alone.

unit.title: Advanced functions, idiomatic Python
unit.description: *args and **kwargs, mutable default trap, generators, itertools, decorators, closures, enumerate and zip, context managers, advanced typing, custom exceptions

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: In a signature, *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs collects keyword arguments into a dict. At call time, * and ** do the reverse: they unpack a sequence or a dict into separate arguments.
cards.example: def log(*args, **kwargs): print(args, kwargs) then log(1, 2, level="info") prints (1, 2) {'level': 'info'}. And requests.get(url, **options) unpacks a dict of options.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: A default value is evaluated only once, when def runs. If it is a list or a dict, the same object is shared by every call and keeps accumulating data. The rule: default to None and create the object inside the body.
cards.example: def add(x, items=None): items = [] if items is None else items; items.append(x); return items. With items=[] as the default, add(1) then add(2) would return [1, 2].

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: A function containing yield returns a generator: it produces values one at a time, on demand, and keeps its state between calls. Ideal for walking through a multi-GB file without loading it all into memory. A generator can only be iterated once.
cards.example: def lines(path): with open(path) as f: for line in f: yield line.strip(); then for l in lines("access.log"): process(l) handles 5 GB of logs without ever loading the whole file into memory.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: An iterator is an object that returns the next element with next() and raises StopIteration at the end; that is what for uses behind the scenes via iter(). The itertools module provides lazy, fast building blocks: chain, islice, groupby, product, count.
cards.example: from itertools import chain, islice; list(islice(chain([1, 2], [3, 4]), 3)) returns [1, 2, 3] without building an intermediate list. islice(gen, 10) takes the first 10 lines of a generator.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns an enhanced version of it (logging, caching, timing, retry). The line @name above a def is equivalent to func = name(func). Add @functools.wraps(func) on the wrapper to keep the name and docstring.
cards.example: @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None) above def fib(n) caches the results: fib(35) drops from about 3 seconds to a few microseconds.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: In Python a function is a first-class object: you can store it in a variable, pass it as an argument or return it. A closure is an inner function that captures the variables of the function that created it, even after that function has returned.
cards.example: def make_counter(): n = 0; def inc(): nonlocal n; n += 1; return n; return inc. Then c = make_counter(); c(); c() returns 2: n lives on inside the closure.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: enumerate(iterable, start=0) yields (index, item) pairs and replaces range(len(...)). zip(a, b) walks several sequences in parallel and stops at the shortest; since Python 3.10, zip(a, b, strict=True) raises ValueError when lengths differ.
cards.example: for i, (name, score) in enumerate(zip(names, scores), start=1): print(f"{i}. {name} : {score}") prints "1. Ana : 92" then "2. Luis : 87", one line per pair.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: Any object defining __enter__ and __exit__ can be used with with: __exit__ runs when the block ends, even if an exception occurs. With contextlib, the @contextmanager decorator turns a generator (setup, yield, cleanup) into a context manager.
cards.example: @contextmanager def timer(label): start = time.perf_counter(); try: yield; finally: print(label, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 2)). Then with timer("parse"): parse(path) prints "parse 0.42", even if parse() raises.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: Since Python 3.9 you write list[str] or dict[str, int] without importing typing; Optional[str] is the same as str | None (3.10+). TypedDict describes the exact shape of a dict (keys and types) so mypy or Pyright can flag errors before runtime.
cards.example: class Report(TypedDict): path: str; rows: int; then def parse(path: str) -> Report | None: return {"path": path, "rows": 3}. mypy rejects report["rowz"] or a rows of type str.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: A class inheriting from Exception (or a subclass such as ValueError) to name a business error. You trigger it with raise and catch it by name, which separates it from Python's own errors. raise MyError() from e keeps the original cause.
cards.example: class InvalidReportError(ValueError): pass; then if not rows: raise InvalidReportError(f"{path}: empty file"); and higher up except InvalidReportError as e: logging.warning(e).

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: A TypeError
exercises.explain: The default list is created only once, at def time: the first call appends 1, the second appends 2 to the same object. With bucket=None and a list created inside the body, you would get [2].

code.src:
def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

add(1)
print(add(2))

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: 3 2 then [1]
3 2 then []
[3, 2, 1] then a StopIteration error
exercises.explain: The generator keeps its position between calls: after two next() calls, only 1 is left to produce. list(gen) consumes that remainder, and the generator is then exhausted.

code.src:
def countdown(n):
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1

gen = countdown(3)
print(next(gen), next(gen))
print(list(gen))

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: A NameError: factor no longer exists after the return
exercises.explain: Each call to multiplier creates a closure that captures its own value of factor: double(5) is 10, triple(5) is 15, so 25 in total.

code.src:
def multiplier(factor):
    def apply(x):
        return x * factor
    return apply

double = multiplier(2)
triple = multiplier(3)
print(double(5) + triple(5))

exercises.prompt: A function reads a report file and returns its line count, or nothing if the file is missing. Which return annotation is correct?
choices: -> int | None (or Optional[int])
-> int (None is accepted by default)
-> Optional (without a type inside)
-> list[int] (an empty list if missing)
exercises.explain: The function can return an integer or None: Optional[int], or int | None since Python 3.10, describes exactly those two cases. -> int hides the None, and Optional alone names no type.

exercises.prompt: A generator that has been fully consumed can be restarted from the beginning with a new for loop.
exercises.explain: An exhausted generator stays empty: a second loop yields nothing. To start over, call the generator function again to get a new object.

exercises.prompt: In a context manager, the __exit__ method runs even if an exception is raised inside the with block.
exercises.explain: That is the whole point of with: cleanup (closing a file, releasing a lock, stopping a timer) is guaranteed, exception or not. With @contextmanager, the code after yield plays that role, protected by try / finally.

exercises.prompt: Put in order the steps to write a @timed decorator that prints the duration of each decorated function.
steps: Define def timed(func): which receives the function to decorate
Inside it, declare def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): preceded by @functools.wraps(func)
In wrapper: record time.perf_counter(), call func(*args, **kwargs), print the duration and return the result
End timed with return wrapper
Apply @timed right above def process_file(path):
exercises.explain: The outer decorator receives func, builds a wrapper that accepts any arguments thanks to *args and **kwargs, then returns it. @timed then replaces process_file with that wrapper, and functools.wraps keeps its name and docstring.

exercises.title: A CLI tool to process reports
exercises.scenario: You are writing report_tool.py, run with python report_tool.py reports/ --out summary.json. It must read 300 CSV report files (some over 2 GB), flag corrupted ones without stopping the run, and print the time spent on each file.

steps.prompt: How do you read each file without exhausting memory?
choices: A generator function read_rows(path) that opens the file with with and yields one line at a time
f.read().splitlines() to load the whole file into a list, then loop over it
Load all 300 files into one big list at startup so the rest goes faster
Start one thread per file, each reading its full content into memory
steps.feedback: The generator keeps only one line in memory at a time: a 2 GB file is processed with a few KB of RAM, and with guarantees the file is closed. The other options load everything, and threads even multiply the problem.

steps.prompt: One file is missing the expected header row. How do you report it cleanly?
choices: Raise an InvalidReportError(ValueError), catch it in the loop, log and continue
Wrap the loop in except Exception: pass so the tool never crashes
print("error") then sys.exit(1) as soon as one file is invalid
Return None and let the calling code guess what went wrong
steps.feedback: A named exception carries a precise message, can be caught without swallowing other errors (a bug or a Ctrl+C stay visible) and lets processing continue. except Exception: pass hides everything, sys.exit stops the other 299 files, and None loses the information.

steps.prompt: How do you measure the time spent on each file without duplicating code everywhere?
choices: A timer(path) context manager built with @contextmanager, used with with around each file
Copy time.perf_counter() at the start and end of every function in the script
Update a global elapsed variable at each step and print it at the end
Print datetime.now() between each step and compute the gaps by hand
steps.feedback: The context manager isolates the measurement in about ten reusable lines. Because the yield sits in a try / finally, the duration is printed even if the file raises InvalidReportError. The other approaches duplicate logic or lose per-file durations.

exercises.explain: A robust CLI tool combines three idioms: a generator to stream reads, a custom exception to report without stopping, and a context manager for clean instrumentation. Add annotations such as list[str] and Report | None, then argparse for the options.

unit.title: Classes and objects
unit.description: class, __init__, self, attributes and methods, __str__, inheritance, super(), @dataclass, @property, class methods, composition

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: A class is a blueprint that describes the data and behavior of a kind of object. An instance is a concrete object built from that blueprint: each instance holds its own values.
cards.example: class Campaign: pass, then summer = Campaign() and winter = Campaign(): one class, two independent instances. type(summer) prints <class '__main__.Campaign'>.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: __init__ is the method Python calls automatically when an instance is created: it sets up its attributes. self refers to the current instance; Python passes it automatically as the first argument of every method.
cards.example: def __init__(self, name, budget): self.name = name; self.budget = budget. Then Campaign("Black Friday", 5000) creates an object whose .budget is 5000.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: An attribute is a piece of data stored in the object (self.budget); a method is a function defined inside the class that acts on that object. Both are reached with a dot: obj.attribute, obj.method().
cards.example: camp.budget returns 5000; camp.spend(1200) runs the spend method, which does self.budget -= 1200. After the call, camp.budget is 3800.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: Two special methods that control how an object is displayed. __str__ returns readable text for print(); __repr__ returns a technical representation, ideally valid code, for the console and debugging. Without __str__, print() falls back to __repr__.
cards.example: def __repr__(self): return f"Campaign({self.name!r}, {self.budget})". Without it or __str__, print(camp) shows <__main__.Campaign object at 0x7f3a2c10>, which is unreadable.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: Inheritance creates a child class that reuses the attributes and methods of a parent class and can extend or override them. super() calls the parent's version, for instance to avoid rewriting __init__.
cards.example: class EmailCampaign(Campaign): def __init__(self, name, budget, list_size): super().__init__(name, budget); self.list_size = list_size. isinstance(e, Campaign) returns True.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: A decorator from the dataclasses module that automatically generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from annotated attributes. Ideal for objects that mostly hold data, with no boilerplate to write.
cards.example: @dataclass class Channel: name: str; cost_per_click: float = 0.5. Channel("Meta") prints as Channel(name='Meta', cost_per_click=0.5) and Channel("Meta") == Channel("Meta") is True.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: A decorator that turns a method into a computed attribute, read without parentheses. It exposes a derived value (or validates assignment with @x.setter) while keeping a simple syntax: obj.total instead of obj.total().
cards.example: @property def remaining(self): return self.budget - self.spent. Then camp.remaining gives 3800 with no parentheses, and is recomputed on every read.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: @classmethod receives the class (cls) instead of the instance: handy for alternative constructors such as from_dict(). @staticmethod receives neither self nor cls: a plain helper function stored inside the class.
cards.example: @classmethod def from_dict(cls, d): return cls(d["name"], d["budget"]). Campaign.from_dict(row) builds a campaign from a CSV row read with csv.DictReader.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: Composition: an object contains other objects (a campaign holds a list of channels). Inheritance: an object is a variant of another. Rule of thumb: "has a" calls for composition, "is a" calls for inheritance.
cards.example: Campaign has Channels: self.channels = [Channel("Google Ads"), Channel("Meta")]. But EmailCampaign is a Campaign: it inherits. Never make Campaign inherit from list!

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: A class pays off when data and the functions that handle it always travel together, or when several objects share the same behavior. For a simple value, a dict or a function is enough.
cards.example: A budget per channel: a dict {"Meta": 2000} is enough. A campaign with 6 channels, an ROI calculation and an export: class Campaign with its methods, clearer than 4 dicts and 8 functions.

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
exercises.explain: a and b are two separate instances: each has its own n attribute, set to 0 in __init__. a.add() is called twice, b.add() only once.

code.src:
class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.n = 0

    def add(self):
        self.n += 1

a = Counter()
b = Counter()
a.add()
a.add()
b.add()
print(a.n, b.n)

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: Channel: Meta
<__main__.Channel object at 0x...>
Meta
Channel('Meta')
exercises.explain: print() calls __str__ when the class defines it. Without __str__ or __repr__, you would get the unreadable memory address <__main__.Channel object at 0x...>.

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: EMAIL PROMO
EMAIL promo
PROMO
AttributeError: EmailCampaign has no attribute name
exercises.explain: EmailCampaign inherits __init__ (so self.name) and overrides label(). super().label() calls the parent's version, which returns "PROMO", then the "EMAIL " prefix is added.

exercises.prompt: You want camp.remaining to return budget - spent, read without parentheses and recomputed on every access. Which decorator do you use?
choices: @property
@dataclass
@staticmethod
@classmethod
exercises.explain: @property turns a method into a computed attribute. @dataclass applies to the whole class, while @staticmethod and @classmethod change what the method receives, not how it is read.

exercises.prompt: self is a reserved Python keyword: the first parameter of a method cannot be named anything else.
exercises.explain: self is only a convention (a strong one, required by PEP 8). Python passes the instance as the first argument whatever it is called, but everyone writes self.

exercises.prompt: With @dataclass, Python automatically generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from the annotated attributes.
exercises.explain: That is the whole point of the decorator: you declare name: str and budget: float, and you get the constructor, a readable display and == comparison without writing a line.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for designing a clean class in order.
steps: Identify the data and behaviors that always go together
Write class and __init__ to initialize the attributes
Add the methods that operate on those attributes
Define __repr__ for a readable display when debugging
Instantiate the class and test each method
exercises.explain: Start from the need (which data, which behaviors), lay the structure with __init__, add the behaviors, polish the display, then check by instantiating.

exercises.title: Modeling campaigns with classes
exercises.scenario: Your marketing team tracks 12 campaigns, each spread across 3 to 6 channels (Google Ads, Meta, email, TikTok) with a budget and spend per channel. Today everything lives in nested dicts and about twenty functions: nobody knows anymore which function expects which structure. You decide to remodel it all with Campaign, Channel and Budget classes.

steps.prompt: How do you represent a channel, which only holds data (name, budget, spent)?
choices: @dataclass class Channel: name: str; budget: float; spent: float = 0.0
Keep a dict {"name": ..., "budget": ..., "spent": ...} per channel
class Channel(dict) to get the best of both
One class per channel: GoogleAds, Meta, Email, TikTok
steps.feedback: An object that mostly stores data is the textbook case for @dataclass: constructor, __repr__ and == for free, named attributes, and a clear error if a field is missing, unlike a dict.

steps.prompt: How should Campaign and Channel relate?
choices: Composition: Campaign keeps self.channels, a list of Channel
Inheritance: class Campaign(Channel) to reuse budget and spent
Reverse inheritance: class Channel(Campaign)
A single Campaign class with one attribute per channel: budget_meta, budget_google…
steps.feedback: A campaign "has" channels, it "is not" a channel: that is composition. A list of Channel accepts 3 or 6 channels without changing the class, and each channel keeps its own budget and spend.

steps.prompt: A campaign's total budget is the sum of its channels' budgets. How do you expose it?
choices: @property def total_budget(self): return sum(c.budget for c in self.channels)
A self.total_budget attribute set in __init__ and updated by hand on every change
A global function total_budget(campaign) outside the class
@staticmethod def total_budget(): return sum(...)
steps.feedback: A @property recomputes the sum on every read: the total can never drift out of sync after a channel is added. The syntax stays camp.total_budget, and a @staticmethod would have no access to self.channels.

exercises.explain: The winning trio: @dataclass for data objects (Channel, Budget), composition to link Campaign to its channels, @property for derived values. Result: 3 readable classes instead of 20 functions and nested dicts.

unit.title: Regex, dates and files
unit.description: re.search / findall / sub, classes and quantifiers, groups, email and UTM, strftime / strptime, timedelta, zoneinfo, ISO 8601, json, csv, pathlib

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: The built-in re module applies regular expressions. re.search() returns the first match (or None), re.findall() returns a list of every match, and re.sub() replaces each match with a replacement string.
cards.example: re.sub(r"\s+", " ", "Hello   big   world") returns "Hello big world": repeated spaces collapse into one. re.search(r"\d+", "Batch 42") returns a Match object whose .group() is "42".

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: A class describes a set of characters: \d (digit), \w (letter, digit or _), \s (whitespace), [a-z] (range), . (anything but a newline). A quantifier says how many times: + (1 or more), * (0 or more), ? (0 or 1), {2,4} (2 to 4).
cards.example: r"\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{4}" matches 14/09/2026; r"\+33 ?\d{9}" matches both +33 612345678 and +33612345678 (the ? makes the space optional).

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: Parentheses capture part of the match, retrieved with m.group(1) or, for a named group (?P<name>\d+), with m.group("name"). With findall(), several groups return tuples; inside re.sub(), \1 reinserts the captured group.
cards.example: m = re.search(r"(?P<year>\d{4})-(?P<month>\d{2})", "2026-09-14"): m.group("month") returns "09" and m.groups() returns ("2026", "09"). re.sub(r"(\d+) €", r"\1 EUR", "Price: 49 €") returns "Price: 49 EUR".

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: To validate an email, re.fullmatch() requires the whole string to fit the pattern (a plain search would accept "x@y.z junk"). To extract UTM parameters from a URL, findall() with two groups returns (key, value) pairs that dict() turns into a dictionary.
cards.example: re.fullmatch(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+", "ana@site.fr") returns a Match, while "ana@site" returns None. dict(re.findall(r"(utm_\w+)=([^&]+)", url)) on ?utm_source=meta&utm_campaign=ete26 gives {"utm_source": "meta", "utm_campaign": "ete26"}.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: datetime.now() returns the current local date and time. strftime() (string from time) turns a datetime into text according to a format: %Y four-digit year, %m month, %d day, %H hour, %M minute, %A full weekday name.
cards.example: datetime.now().strftime("%d/%m/%Y %H:%M") returns "14/09/2026 09:30". To name a dated file with no forbidden character: f"report_{datetime.now():%Y%m%d}.csv" gives report_20260914.csv.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: strptime() (string parse time) is the reverse of strftime(): it reads text with the given format and returns a datetime, or raises ValueError if it does not fit. timedelta is a duration you add to or subtract from a date; subtracting two datetimes gives a timedelta.
cards.example: d = datetime.strptime("14/09/2026", "%d/%m/%Y"); (d + timedelta(days=30)).date() returns 2026-10-14 and (d - datetime(2026, 1, 1)).days returns 256. Handy to follow up a lead 7 days after sign-up.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: A "naive" datetime has no time zone; ZoneInfo("Europe/Paris") (zoneinfo module, standard since Python 3.9) makes it "aware". ISO 8601 is the universal exchange format, 2026-09-14T09:30:00+02:00, produced by isoformat() and read back by fromisoformat().
cards.example: paris = datetime(2026, 9, 14, 9, 30, tzinfo=ZoneInfo("Europe/Paris")); paris.isoformat() gives "2026-09-14T09:30:00+02:00" and paris.astimezone(ZoneInfo("America/New_York")) shows 03:30 for the same instant. APIs (Stripe, HubSpot, GA4) exchange dates in ISO 8601, often in UTC (Z suffix).

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: json.loads() turns JSON text into Python objects (dict, list, str, int, bool, None); json.dumps() does the reverse. indent=2 makes the output readable, ensure_ascii=False keeps accented characters; json.load() and json.dump() work directly on an open file.
cards.example: json.dumps({"city": "Genève", "leads": 42}, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False) writes "Genève" as is instead of "Gen\u00e8ve". json.loads('{"ok": true, "total": null}') returns {"ok": True, "total": None}.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: csv.DictReader reads a CSV file and returns each row as a dict whose keys are the headers from the first line. csv.DictWriter writes dicts: declare fieldnames, call writeheader() then writerow(). delimiter=";" handles French Excel exports.
cards.example: with open("leads.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f: rows = list(csv.DictReader(f, delimiter=";")) then rows[0]["email"]. Always pass newline="" to avoid blank lines on Windows.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: pathlib.Path represents a file path in an object-oriented, portable way (Windows, macOS, Linux). The / operator joins segments; .exists(), .suffix, .stem, .glob("*.csv"), .read_text() and .write_text() are a cleaner alternative to os.path and open().
cards.example: out = Path("exports") / "leads_clean.csv"; out.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True) creates the folder if needed; out.suffix is ".csv", out.stem is "leads_clean" and list(Path("exports").glob("*.csv")) lists every CSV in the folder.

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: 2 bob@shop.com
2 ana@site.fr
1 ana@site.fr
An IndexError
exercises.explain: re.findall() returns the list of every match, here two emails; index 1 is the second element, bob@shop.com.

code.src:
import re
text = "Contact: ana@site.fr, bob@shop.com"
emails = re.findall(r"[\w.-]+@[\w.-]+\.\w+", text)
print(len(emails), emails[1])

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: newsletter
utm_source=newsletter
newsletter&utm_medium=email
None
exercises.explain: m.group(1) returns only the content of the first capture group; \w+ stops at & because that character is not a letter, digit or _. m.group(0) would have given the whole match.

code.src:
import re
url = "https://x.com/?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=email"
m = re.search(r"utm_source=(\w+)", url)
print(m.group(1))

exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
choices: A ValueError
exercises.explain: strptime parses the ISO date, timedelta(days=1) removes one day (2026 is not a leap year, February ends on the 28th) and strftime rewrites it as day/month/year.

code.src:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
d = datetime.strptime("2026-03-01", "%Y-%m-%d")
print((d - timedelta(days=1)).strftime("%d/%m/%Y"))

exercises.prompt: Which statement returns the current time in Paris with its time zone (an "aware" datetime)?
choices: datetime.now(ZoneInfo("Europe/Paris"))
datetime.now("Europe/Paris")
datetime.now().timezone("Europe/Paris")
datetime.utcnow(tz="Europe/Paris")
exercises.explain: datetime.now() accepts a tzinfo object, which ZoneInfo from the standard zoneinfo module provides. A plain string raises TypeError, .timezone() does not exist and utcnow() has been deprecated since Python 3.12.

exercises.prompt: re.search() scans the whole string and returns the list of every match found.
exercises.explain: re.search() stops at the first match and returns a Match object (or None). re.findall() is the one that returns the list of every match.

exercises.prompt: With csv.DictReader, each row read is a dictionary whose keys are the headers from the first line of the file.
exercises.explain: That is the whole point of DictReader compared with csv.reader: you write row["email"] instead of row[2], which survives a change in column order.

exercises.prompt: Put in order the steps of a script that cleans a CSV export of leads and produces a clean file.
steps: Open the file with Path("exports/leads.csv") and read the rows with csv.DictReader
Normalize each email (strip + lower), validate it with re.fullmatch() and discard invalid rows
On the remaining rows, convert the mixed date formats with strptime() then rewrite them in ISO 8601 with isoformat()
Deduplicate on the normalized email, keeping for each email only the row with the earliest ISO date
Write the result with csv.DictWriter (writeheader then writerows)
exercises.explain: Read first, normalize and filter the emails, convert the dates of the remaining rows, then deduplicate: the key is the normalized email (otherwise Ana@Site.fr and ana@site.fr both get through) and choosing which row to keep requires dates already in ISO, hence comparable. Write the clean file last.

exercises.title: Cleaning a leads export
exercises.scenario: The CRM exported 3,200 trade-show leads into leads.csv (";" separator). Opening it, you see emails like "ana@site" or "n/a", sign-up dates written as "03/07/2026", "2026-07-03" or "3 juil. 2026", and the same contact entered several times with different capitalization. Sales wants a clean file tomorrow morning.

steps.prompt: How do you reliably discard invalid emails?
choices: You normalize, then re.fullmatch(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+", email)
You keep the row if "@" in email: that is enough
You use re.search(r"\w+@\w+", email): if it finds something, the email is fine
You only keep emails ending in ".com" or ".fr"
steps.feedback: fullmatch requires the whole string to fit the pattern: "ana@site" (no domain) and "n/a" are rejected. The "@ in email" test lets "ana@site" through, search accepts "x@y junk", and filtering on .com/.fr throws away valid emails (.io, .ch, .co.uk).

steps.prompt: The sign-up dates mix three formats. How do you standardize them?
choices: You try each format with strptime() and try / except, then ISO 8601
You do date.replace("/", "-"): every date will have dashes
You leave the dates as they are: sales can read them
You delete the date column to avoid errors
steps.feedback: strptime with a list of formats ("%d/%m/%Y", "%Y-%m-%d", and for "3 juil. 2026" a %b format with the French locale or a table of abbreviated months) converts everything into datetime; ISO 8601 (2026-07-03) then sorts correctly, even as text. replace does not fix day/month order, and leaving or deleting the column prevents any calculation (follow-up at D+7, lead age).

steps.prompt: How do you remove duplicates without losing real contacts?
choices: You deduplicate on the normalized email (strip + lower) with a "seen" set
You do list(set(rows)) on the list of dictionaries
You compare first names: two "Ana" are necessarily the same person
You compare emails as they are, without changing them, to stay faithful to the export
steps.feedback: The normalized email is the most reliable key: "Ana@Site.fr" and "ana@site.fr " point to the same mailbox. set(rows) raises TypeError because a dict is not hashable, the first name alone merges different people, and comparing without normalizing lets capitalized duplicates through.

exercises.explain: A robust clean-up always chains the same building blocks: csv.DictReader to read, re.fullmatch to validate, strptime then isoformat to normalize dates, a set of normalized emails to deduplicate, csv.DictWriter to write. On 3,200 rows this script runs in under a second and can be rerun on every export.

unit.title: SQL from Python
unit.description: SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE, keys, indexes, sqlite3, parameterized queries, pd.read_sql, ORM

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: SELECT picks the columns, FROM the table, WHERE filters rows, ORDER BY sorts them (ASC or DESC) and LIMIT caps the number of results. This is the skeleton of the vast majority of read queries.
cards.example: SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price > 50 ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 5; returns the 5 most expensive products among those above 50 €.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: JOIN combines two tables on a shared column. INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match on both sides; LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table and fills with NULL when nothing matches on the right.
cards.example: SELECT c.name, o.total FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id; lists every customer, including those with no order (total is NULL). With INNER JOIN they would disappear.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: GROUP BY gathers rows that share a value, then an aggregate (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) computes one figure per group. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, whereas WHERE filters rows before it.
cards.example: SELECT channel, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM sales GROUP BY channel HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000; gives revenue per channel, keeping only channels above 1000 €.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: The three write statements: INSERT INTO adds a row, UPDATE … SET changes columns, DELETE FROM removes rows. Without a WHERE clause, UPDATE and DELETE affect every row in the table, with no confirmation.
cards.example: UPDATE products SET price = 19.90 WHERE id = 42; changes a single price. Forgetting the WHERE would set every product in the catalog to 19.90.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: The primary key (PRIMARY KEY) identifies each row uniquely, often an auto-incremented integer. A foreign key (FOREIGN KEY) points to the primary key of another table and guarantees that the reference exists.
cards.example: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER REFERENCES customers(id)); in SQLite you must run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON for the constraint to actually be enforced.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: An index is a sorted structure (usually a B-tree) the engine consults to locate rows without scanning the whole table. It speeds up WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY on the indexed column but slightly slows down every write.
cards.example: CREATE INDEX idx_sales_channel ON sales(channel); on 10 million rows, a WHERE channel = 'email' filter drops from several seconds to a few milliseconds.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: Standard library module: sqlite3.connect() opens (or creates) a .db file, cursor() gives you a cursor, execute() runs a query, fetchall() reads the results and commit() saves writes to disk.
cards.example: con = sqlite3.connect('shop.db'); cur = con.cursor(); cur.execute('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales'); print(cur.fetchone()[0]); con.close() prints the number of sales, nothing to install.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: Building a query by concatenating user-supplied text opens the door to SQL injection: "' OR 1=1 --" bypasses a filter. With parameters (? in sqlite3), the value is sent separately and never interpreted as SQL.
cards.example: cur.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?', (email,)) is safe; f"… WHERE email = '{email}'" is not. The tuple (email,) keeps its comma even with a single parameter.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: pd.read_sql(query, connection) runs a SQL query and returns a DataFrame whose columns are named after the SELECT. Ideal for letting the database filter and aggregate, then analyzing or plotting the result in pandas.
cards.example: df = pd.read_sql('SELECT channel, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM sales GROUP BY channel', con) then df.plot.bar(x='channel', y='revenue'): 3 rows received instead of 2 million.

cards.subject: python
cards.definition: An ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) represents tables as Python classes and rows as objects; SQLAlchemy generates the SQL. Useful for an application with many models and writes; overkill for an analysis script or a one-off report.
cards.example: class Sale(Base): __tablename__ = 'sales' with id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True), then session.scalars(select(Sale).where(Sale.channel == 'email')).all(): not a single line of hand-written SQL.

exercises.prompt: After this script runs, what does the sales table contain?
choices: Nothing new: without con.commit(), the insert is rolled back on close
A new row ('email', 120), execute() writes straight to disk
An error: execute() does not accept a tuple as second argument
Two new rows, one for each question mark
exercises.explain: With sqlite3, writes stay in an open transaction until you call con.commit(); closing the connection without committing discards them. The parameter tuple is the correct form.

code.src:
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect("shop.db")
cur = con.cursor()
cur.execute(
    "INSERT INTO sales (channel, amount) VALUES (?, ?)",
    ("email", 120),
)
con.close()

exercises.prompt: Does a customer who never placed an order appear in the result, and with which nb_orders value?
choices: Yes, with nb_orders = 0: LEFT JOIN keeps it and COUNT(o.id) ignores NULLs
No, LEFT JOIN drops rows with no match in orders
Yes, with nb_orders = 1, because the customer row counts as one
Yes, with nb_orders = NULL, since no order exists
exercises.explain: LEFT JOIN keeps every customers row and fills o.id with NULL when there is no order. COUNT(column) skips NULLs, so the customer shows up with 0. With COUNT(*) it would be 1.

code.src:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS nb_orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id;

exercises.prompt: What is wrong with this code?
choices: SQL injection: use a ? placeholder and a tuple (email,)
Nothing, an f-string is the recommended way to pass a value to SQL
A SyntaxError: single quotes are not allowed in a SQL query
execute() rejects queries that contain SELECT *
exercises.explain: The user's input is glued into the query and interpreted as SQL. The safe form is cur.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?', (email,)): sqlite3 passes the value separately and never executes it.

code.src:
email = input("Email: ")
query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'"
cur.execute(query)
rows = cur.fetchall()

exercises.prompt: This query takes 6 seconds on a sales table with 10 million rows. Which statement, run only once, makes it almost instant?
choices: CREATE INDEX idx_sales_channel ON sales(channel);
Add ORDER BY channel to the query so the engine sorts first
Declare amount as the table's PRIMARY KEY
Add LIMIT 1000 at the end of the query
exercises.explain: Without an index, the engine reads all 10 million rows to test channel. An index on channel lets it jump straight to the 'email' rows. LIMIT would break the sum and ORDER BY would add work.

exercises.prompt: DELETE FROM sales; without a WHERE clause removes every row from the sales table.
exercises.explain: True. UPDATE and DELETE apply to every row when no WHERE restricts them. Before a write, test your WHERE with a SELECT to check which rows are targeted.

exercises.prompt: pd.read_sql() always loads the whole table into memory: you then have to filter and aggregate in pandas.
exercises.explain: False. pd.read_sql() runs whatever query you give it: with WHERE and GROUP BY, the database does the heavy lifting and pandas only receives the result, for example 3 rows instead of 2 million.

exercises.prompt: Put in order the steps to get a DataFrame of sales per channel from a SQLite database.
steps: con = sqlite3.connect('shop.db') opens the connection to the file
Write the query SELECT channel, SUM(amount) FROM sales WHERE sold_at >= ? GROUP BY channel
df = pd.read_sql(query, con, params=(start_date,)) returns the aggregated DataFrame
Export or plot the result, for example df.to_csv('report.csv')
con.close() releases the connection once the report is produced
exercises.explain: Open the connection, let SQL filter and aggregate with a safe parameter, pandas receives a result ready to export, then close the connection cleanly.

exercises.title: The sales-per-channel report
exercises.scenario: Nova Café's marketing team must deliver every Monday the week's revenue per channel (website, app, marketplace). The data lives in sales.db, table sales (id, channel, amount, sold_at), 2 million rows. The intern suggests pd.read_sql('SELECT * FROM sales', con) followed by a groupby in pandas.

steps.prompt: Which approach do you pick to compute revenue per channel?
choices: A GROUP BY inside pd.read_sql: the database aggregates, pandas gets 3 rows
SELECT * then df.groupby('channel')['amount'].sum(): 2 million rows in memory
A Python loop running one SELECT per channel and summing amounts by hand
Export the whole database to CSV, then pd.read_csv() and a pivot_table
steps.feedback: Letting SQL do GROUP BY and SUM is the rule: the engine is built for it and only the result travels to Python. Loading 2 million rows to keep 3 wastes memory and time.

steps.prompt: The report must cover only the last 7 days, with a start date typed by the user. How do you add it?
choices: Add WHERE sold_at >= ? and pass params=(start_date,) to pd.read_sql
Insert the date with an f-string: f"WHERE sold_at >= '{start_date}'"
Keep the query without WHERE and filter the dates in pandas after loading
Hard-code the date in the query and edit it by hand every Monday
steps.feedback: A ? placeholder with params= is both safe (no SQL injection) and clean: the date changes without editing the query text. The f-string would work but exposes the database to any malicious input.

steps.prompt: The filtered query still takes 8 seconds: sold_at is not indexed. What do you do?
choices: Run once CREATE INDEX idx_sales_sold_at ON sales(sold_at) then con.commit()
Rewrite the script with SQLAlchemy ORM, which optimizes queries
Add LIMIT 1000 to the query to read fewer rows
Drop the id primary key to make the table lighter
steps.feedback: An index on sold_at lets the engine jump straight to the week's rows instead of scanning 2 million. An ORM does not make a query faster, LIMIT would corrupt the total and the primary key is not the issue.

exercises.explain: The right reflex in three moves: aggregate on the SQL side (GROUP BY), pass variable values as parameters (?) and index the filtered columns. For a weekly report, sqlite3 + pd.read_sql are more than enough; the ORM can wait for a real application.

unit.title: CSS: typography and transforms
unit.description: clamp(), line-height, letter-spacing, type scale, margin, gap, max-width in ch, transform, overflow, object-fit, aspect-ratio

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: clamp(min, preferred, max) scales a size between two bounds according to viewport width, with no media query. The preferred value usually mixes rem and vw so text stays readable and still respects user zoom.
cards.example: h1 { font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 1rem + 3vw, 3.5rem); }: 28 px on a 360 px phone, then 56 px once the viewport passes 1,333 px.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: line-height sets the height of each line of text. Written without a unit (1.5), it multiplies each element's own font size. Vertical rhythm means aligning line heights and margins on the same repeating step.
cards.example: body { line-height: 1.5; } gives 24 px lines for 16 px text; paragraphs spaced with 1.5rem (24 px) fall back onto the same 24 px grid.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: letter-spacing adds or removes space between letters; text-transform changes the displayed case (uppercase, capitalize) without touching the HTML. Uppercase text reads better with a little extra spacing.
cards.example: .eyebrow { text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 0.08em; font-size: 0.75rem; }: a small uppercase kicker with 0.96 px between letters.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: A type scale derives every size from a base (16 px) multiplied by a constant ratio: 1.25 (major fourth), 1.333 or 1.5. It guarantees a consistent hierarchy and keeps the number of sizes small.
cards.example: Ratio 1.25: 16 → 20 → 25 → 31.25 → 39 px. In CSS: --step-1: calc(var(--step-0) * 1.25); then h2 { font-size: var(--step-2); }.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: margin pushes an element away from its neighbors; padding pushes content away from the edge of its own box, background and border included. gap spaces the children of a flex or grid container with no stray space before the first or after the last.
cards.example: .card { padding: 1.5rem; } .list { display: flex; gap: 1rem; }: 16 px between cards, and zero wasted space before the first one or after the last.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: The ch unit equals the width of the digit 0 in the current font. Capping text at 60-75ch yields lines of roughly 45 to 90 characters, the comfortable range for the eye; beyond that, readers lose their place at line breaks.
cards.example: p { max-width: 65ch; margin-inline: auto; }: paragraphs top out at 65 characters wide and stay centred, even on a 1,920 px screen.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: transform moves (translate), resizes (scale) or rotates (rotate) an element without changing the flow or its neighbors. The browser applies it at the compositing stage, often on the GPU, with no layout recalculation: ideal for 60 fps animation.
cards.example: .btn:hover { transform: translateY(-2px) scale(1.03); }: the button lifts without shifting the rest of the page, unlike margin-top: -2px.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: overflow decides what happens to content that spills out of its box: visible, hidden or auto (scrollbar when needed). text-overflow: ellipsis replaces the end of a clipped line with '…', provided the text is kept on a single hidden line.
cards.example: .title { white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; }: 'Complete guide to typography' becomes 'Complete guide to typ…' in a narrow column.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: object-fit controls how an image or video fills its box when the proportions differ: cover crops to fill without distortion, contain keeps the whole image with empty bands, fill stretches it (avoid).
cards.example: .avatar { width: 64px; height: 64px; object-fit: cover; object-position: center top; }: an 800 × 1,200 px portrait is cropped from the top, never squashed.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: aspect-ratio fixes a box's width-to-height ratio (16 / 9, 1 / 1). Height follows from width: no more padding-top: 56.25% hack, and the space is reserved before content loads, which prevents layout shift.
cards.example: .video { width: 100%; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; }: a 360 px wide YouTube player is automatically 202.5 px tall, before the iframe even loads.

exercises.prompt: On a 1,000 px wide viewport (1rem = 16 px), what size does this heading get?
choices: 56 px
64 px
32 px
40 px
exercises.explain: The preferred value is 16 px + 4% of 1,000 px = 56 px. It sits between the minimum (2rem = 32 px) and the maximum (4rem = 64 px), so clamp() keeps it as is.

exercises.prompt: This title should stay on a single line and end with '…' when it is too long, but it simply wraps and no '…' appears. Which declaration is missing?
choices: white-space: nowrap;
display: block;
overflow-x: scroll;
text-wrap: balance;
exercises.explain: text-overflow: ellipsis only acts on a line that overflows horizontally. Without white-space: nowrap the text wraps onto several lines, nothing overflows, so no ellipsis is drawn.

exercises.prompt: This hover effect makes the page stutter and shifts the neighbouring cards. Which rewrite fixes both problems?
choices: transform: translateY(-8px);
position: relative; top: -8px;
padding-top: 8px;
transition-timing-function: linear;
exercises.explain: margin-top changes the flow: the browser recalculates layout and the neighbors move. position: relative; top no longer moves the neighbors, but top still triggers a layout pass on every frame, so it still stutters. transform is handled at compositing, with no layout pass: the animation stays smooth and isolated to the card.

exercises.prompt: A 1,200 × 800 px photo must fill this square thumbnail without distortion and without empty bands. Which declaration should you add?
choices: object-fit: cover;
object-fit: contain;
object-fit: fill;
aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
exercises.explain: cover scales the image until it covers the whole box while keeping its proportions, then crops the excess. contain would leave empty bands top and bottom; fill (the default) would squash the photo.

exercises.prompt: A unitless line-height (1.5) is recomputed from each element's own font size, whereas line-height: 24px stays fixed everywhere, even inside a 40 px heading.
exercises.explain: True: the unitless value is inherited as a factor, so a 40 px h2 gets 60 px lines. With an inherited 24px, the heading's lines would overlap.

exercises.prompt: On a flex container, gap also adds space before the first child and after the last one, exactly like a margin set on every child.
exercises.explain: False: gap only spaces children from each other. That is precisely its advantage over margin, which forces you to cancel the first or last item's margin with :first-child or :last-child.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for building a fluid, readable typographic system in the right order.
steps: Pick the body base size (16 px) and a scale ratio (1.25)
Compute the levels (20, 25, 31, 39 px) and store them in --step-1 to --step-4 variables
Make each level fluid with clamp() between a mobile value and a desktop value
Set line-height (1.5 for body text, 1.2 for headings) to lock the vertical rhythm
Cap paragraphs with max-width: 65ch and check the result on a 375 px phone
exercises.explain: Start from the base and ratio, derive the scale, make it fluid, set the line height, then cap the measure before testing on a phone.

exercises.title: A landing page unreadable on mobile
exercises.scenario: You take over a SaaS startup's landing page. On desktop everything looks fine, but on mobile (375 px) the font-size: 64px heading overflows the screen, paragraphs stretch across the full width with 120-character lines on tablet, and the 14 px text with line-height: 14px is cramped. The mobile bounce rate is at 78%.

steps.prompt: The 64 px heading overflows on mobile but must stay bold on desktop. What do you do?
choices: font-size: clamp(2rem, 1.2rem + 4vw, 4rem), fluid from 32 to 64 px
Add overflow: hidden on the heading to hide whatever overflows
Shrink the heading to 20 px everywhere, desktop included
Apply transform: scale(0.5) to the heading on mobile
steps.feedback: clamp() yields about 34 px at 375 px wide and climbs back to 64 px on large screens, with no media query. Hiding the overflow or shrinking everywhere sacrifices content; scale() does not free the space taken in the flow.

steps.prompt: On tablet, paragraphs run 120 characters per line and readers lose their place at line breaks. What is the fix?
choices: Cap paragraphs with max-width: 65ch; margin-inline: auto;
Set paragraphs to text-align: justify for more even lines
Set letter-spacing: -0.05em to fit more words per line
Add a media query that drops the font to 12 px on tablet
steps.feedback: max-width in ch caps the line at about 65 characters whatever the screen size, and margin-inline: auto centers it. Justifying creates rivers of white space; tightening letters or shrinking the font makes readability worse.

steps.prompt: The 14 px body text with line-height: 14px is cramped and tiring. What do you change?
choices: font-size: 1rem and line-height: 1.5, with spaced-out paragraphs
Keep 14 px but set text-transform: uppercase to open up the text

Insert
tags between lines with 8 px of padding
Force line-height: 14px !important to make the rendering uniform
steps.feedback:
16 px with a 1.5 line height gives 24 px lines, and 1.5rem margins carry that 24 px rhythm between paragraphs. Uppercase slows reading,
tags break responsiveness and !important locks the problem in place.

exercises.explain: Readable mobile typography rests on three settings: a fluid size with clamp(), a measure capped in ch, and a proportional line height that sets a steady vertical rhythm.

unit.title: CSS: organize and scale
unit.description: BEM, @layer, container queries, :has(), nesting, Tailwind, Sass, reset, critical CSS, DevTools

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: Class naming method based on Block, Element and Modifier (block__element--modifier). Each component is self-contained, with no nested selectors: specificity stays flat and the names explain themselves.
cards.example: .card, .card__title, .card--featured: at a glance you know --featured is a variant of the card, and .card__title never depends on its parent. One class per rule, so no specificity wars.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: The @layer rule groups styles into ordered layers (reset, base, components, utilities). Layer order beats specificity, and unlayered styles always win over styles declared inside a layer.
cards.example: @layer reset, base, components, utilities; then @layer components { .btn { … } }: a .btn class in utilities beats #header .btn in base, despite the id. Supported by all browsers since March 2022.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: @container query that adapts a component to the size of its parent container, not the viewport. The parent declares container-type: inline-size; the component becomes reusable in a sidebar as well as at full width.
cards.example: .card-wrapper { container-type: inline-size; } @container (min-width: 400px) { .card { display: flex; } }; the cqw and cqi units measure the container. Full support since Firefox 110 (February 2023).

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: :has() selects a parent based on its children (the "parent selector"). :is() groups selectors and takes the specificity of the strongest one; :where() does the same with zero specificity, ideal for styles that are easy to override.
cards.example: .form:has(:invalid) { border-color: red; } colors the whole form as soon as one field is invalid, with no JavaScript. :where(h1, h2, h3) { margin: 0; } can be overridden by a single class. :has() has been supported everywhere since Firefox 121 (December 2023).

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: Ability to write rules inside other rules directly in CSS, without a preprocessor. The & symbol stands for the parent selector (.btn { &:hover { … } }). Supported by all browsers since late 2023.
cards.example: .card { padding: 1rem; & .title { font-weight: 700; } &:hover { box-shadow: 0 4px 12px #0002; } @media (width >= 768px) { padding: 2rem; } }: media queries nest too. Careful: nesting too deep brings back the specificity that BEM was avoiding.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: Framework of utility classes (flex, p-4, text-lg) applied directly in the HTML. The build keeps only the classes actually used, so the final CSS is very small. Relevant for a team shipping component-based interfaces fast.
cards.example: <button class="px-4 py-2 rounded bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-700"> replaces a hand-written .btn class. Tailwind v4 (January 2025) is configured in CSS via @theme and often outputs less than 10 KB in production. Avoid it on a 3-page brochure site with no build step.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: Sass is a preprocessor compiled to CSS: its variables ($gap), mixins and functions exist only at build time. A custom property (--gap) lives in the browser, inherits through the cascade and can be changed by JavaScript or in a media query.
cards.example: $breakpoint-md: 768px; is still useful because a media query does not accept var(). For a theme, prefer --color-primary: changing one class on <html> switches the whole site. With native nesting and color-mix(), many teams are dropping Sass in 2026.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: Stylesheet loaded first to neutralize browser default styles. A reset wipes everything (margins, bullets), normalize.css only harmonizes differences between browsers. Modern resets fit in 50 lines.
cards.example: *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; } body { margin: 0; line-height: 1.5; } img { max-width: 100%; display: block; }: the core of a modern reset. Put it in @layer reset so it loses against everything else.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: The browser paints nothing until the CSS referenced in <head> is downloaded and parsed: it blocks rendering. Critical CSS means inlining the styles of the visible area and loading the rest deferred.
cards.example: A 10 KB <style> of critical CSS in <head>, then <link rel="stylesheet" href="main.css" media="print" onload="this.media='all'"> for the rest. Lighthouse flags it in the "Eliminate render-blocking resources" audit; critical or Beasties (formerly critters) automate it.

cards.subject: css
cards.definition: Tools built into Chrome to diagnose CSS. The Styles panel shows crossed-out (overridden) rules, the Computed tab gives the final value of each property and where it comes from, Lighthouse scores performance and best practices.
cards.example: A heading stays blue despite your rule? Computed > color > arrow: you see that #header h1 (specificity 1,0,1) wins. The Coverage tab often reveals 70 to 90% of CSS never used on a page; Lighthouse aims for a score above 90.

exercises.prompt: A link <a class="btn"> sits inside <nav id="nav">. What color does it show?
choices: Green: the unlayered rule always wins over the layers
Red: #nav .btn has the highest specificity
Blue: components is declared after base
Red: the base layer is written last in the file
exercises.explain: Unlayered styles beat any layer, regardless of specificity. Without the green rule, blue would win: components comes after base in the declared order, and layer order beats the id.

exercises.prompt: What color does an <a> placed inside <ul class="nav"> get?
choices: Black: :where() has zero specificity, both rules tie and the last one wins
Gray: .nav makes the first rule more specific
Gray: :where() takes the specificity of the #menu id
Black: :where() only targets elements that match both selectors
exercises.explain: :where(.nav, #menu) a scores (0,0,1), exactly like a. With equal specificity, the rule written last wins. With :is() instead, specificity would be (1,0,1) and the link would be gray.

code.src:
:where(.nav, #menu) a { color: gray; }

a { color: black; }

exercises.prompt: A .card is placed inside .sidebar. When does it switch to display: flex?
choices: Once .sidebar is 400 px wide or more, whatever the viewport
As soon as the browser window is at least 400 px wide
As soon as .card itself is at least 400 px wide
Never: a @container requires a container name
exercises.explain: The queried container is the nearest ancestor with container-type, here .sidebar. The component reacts to the space it is given, not the screen: that is what makes it reusable anywhere. The name (container-name) is optional.

exercises.prompt: Following the BEM convention, how do you name a card's title, and its "featured" variant?
choices: .card__title for the element and .card--featured for the variant
.card .title for the element and .card.featured for the variant
.card--title for the element and .card__featured for the variant
#card-title for the element and .featured for the variant
exercises.explain: Two underscores for the element (part of the block), two hyphens for the modifier (variant). Each rule targets a single class: no descendant, no id, so specificity stays flat and predictable.

exercises.prompt: A Sass variable like $gap can be changed by JavaScript in the browser, exactly like a custom property.
exercises.explain: False: $gap is replaced by its value at compile time and no longer exists in the shipped CSS. Only a custom property (--gap) lives in the browser and can be read or changed with style.setProperty().

exercises.prompt: A CSS file referenced by <link> in <head> prevents the page from being displayed until it is downloaded and parsed.
exercises.explain: True: CSS is a render-blocking resource, the browser waits to avoid a flash of unstyled page. Hence the value of inlining critical CSS and deferring the rest with media="print" then onload.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps in order to set up critical CSS on a home page.
steps: Measure the starting point: Lighthouse score, LCP and the "render-blocking resources" audit
Extract the styles of the visible area with a tool like critical or critters
Inline that critical CSS in a <style> tag inside <head>
Load the rest of the stylesheet deferred (media="print" then onload)
Run Lighthouse again and compare LCP before and after
exercises.explain: Measure first, otherwise you cannot prove the gain. Extract, inline then defer is the technical order; keep the inlined block small (about 10 to 14 KB) so it fits in the first network packets.

exercises.title: The 8,000-line stylesheet
exercises.scenario: You join the front-end team of an invoicing SaaS. The main.css file is 8,000 lines long, piled up over 4 years by 6 developers. It contains 340 !important, selectors like #app .content div.table tr td span, and every fix breaks something else somewhere. Nobody dares delete a line. Management refuses a full rewrite: the product must keep shipping features every sprint.

steps.prompt: What do you start with in the first week?
choices: Measure first: Coverage and Lighthouse on the 5 most visited screens
Migrate all the HTML to Tailwind during a dedicated sprint, with no other delivery
Add !important on the rules that break to stabilize things quickly
Convert main.css to Sass with partials, without changing a single rule
steps.feedback: Correct. Coverage typically reveals 70 to 90% of rules never applied on a given screen: you get hard numbers to convince and prioritize. Rewriting in Tailwind blocks deliveries, !important deepens the debt, and splitting into Sass removes nothing.

steps.prompt: How do you structure the CSS so new code stops fighting the old one?
choices: Put main.css in a legacy @layer and the new BEM code in components
Write new rules with ids and longer chains to make sure they win
Create one CSS file per developer to avoid merge conflicts
Put all new components in inline styles in the HTML
steps.feedback: Well spotted. Since layer order beats specificity, a simple .invoice__total class in components overrides #app .content … span in legacy. The legacy becomes a quarantine zone, and new code stays flat and readable.

steps.prompt: How do you shrink the file without breaking production, and keep the debt from coming back?
choices: Delete unused CSS in batches under visual tests, with Stylelint in CI
Delete the 5,000 suspicious lines all at once on a Friday evening and fix on Monday if needed
Forbid any new CSS: developers can only use existing classes
Minify main.css to save weight and consider the problem solved
steps.feedback: Perfect. Progressive deletion, protected by compared screenshots, turns a risk into a routine. Linting in CI keeps the 340 !important from becoming 400. Minification changes nothing about maintainability.

exercises.explain: Scaling legacy CSS means measuring, isolating the old code in a low layer, writing new code in BEM, then deleting in small batches protected by tests and linting. No full rewrite, and deliveries keep flowing.

unit.title: HTML: forms, tables, links
unit.description: form and method, input types, label, select and textarea, native validation, button, table, links, lists, global attributes

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: On <form>, action sets the URL that receives the data and method the HTTP verb: GET puts the fields in the URL (search, filters), POST sends them in the request body (sign-up, payment).
cards.example: <form action="/signup" method="post">: a password must never travel via GET, or it shows up in the URL, the history and the server logs.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: The type attribute changes how the field behaves: email and number check the format, date opens a calendar, checkbox allows several choices, radio only one among the buttons sharing the same name.
cards.example: <input type="email" name="email"> shows a mobile keyboard with @ and .com; <input type="number" name="qty"> opens the numeric keypad.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: <label> names a field. Its for attribute matches the id of the <input>: clicking the text focuses the field and the screen reader announces the label. A placeholder never replaces a label.
cards.example: <label for="email">Your email</label> <input id="email" type="email">: the clickable area grows and Lighthouse stops flagging "Form elements do not have associated labels".

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: <select> renders a drop-down list where each <option> carries a value sent to the server; selected sets the default choice. <textarea> captures long, multi-line text and has no value attribute.
cards.example: <select name="country"><option value="fr" selected>France</option><option value="es">Spain</option></select> then <textarea name="message" rows="4"></textarea>.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: The browser blocks submission if a required field is empty, if the value falls outside min / max or minlength / maxlength, or if it fails the regular expression in pattern. Zero JavaScript, but always re-validate on the server.
